# Dmint — Complete Documentation (Full Text Corpus)
> Dmint is a deterministic security authorization and enforcement engine for AI-agent tool calls.
> Website: https://dmint.app | Docs: https://docs.dmint.app


================================================================================
DOCUMENT: Overview
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/
SECTION: Get Started
SUMMARY: Dmint is a deterministic authorization layer for AI agent tool calls with cryptographic request binding and single-use human approvals.
================================================================================

# Deterministic Security for AI Agent Tool Calls

Dmint places a deterministic, code-governed authorization boundary between AI agents and privileged execution environments—covering **native coding-agent hooks** (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI, OpenCode, Cursor, Windsurf, Cline), **MCP servers**, and **Python functions**.

---

## The Problem

Autonomous agents frequently possess high-privilege access to execute shell commands, query databases, edit files, and call external APIs.

Prompt-based guardrails (*"Please do not run `DELETE` or `git push` without asking"*) fail when an agent encounters prompt injection, jailbreaks, or context drift:

```text
Without Dmint (Probabilistic):
AI Model ────[ System Prompt / Model Guardrail ]────► Executes DROP TABLE / RM -RF

With Dmint (Deterministic & Fail-Closed):
AI Model ────► Tool Call ────► [ Dmint Policy Engine ] ────► ALLOW: Executes tool
                                      │
                                      ├─► DENY: Fails closed immediately
                                      └─► APPROVAL_REQUIRED: Halts until signed, single-use human approval
```

Dmint evaluates every tool request against deterministic, declarative policies before the protected capability runs. There is **zero LLM evaluation** in the runtime authorization decision path.

---

## 30-Second Setup for Coding Agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor)

Protect built-in shell and file tools in your coding agent with one command:

```bash
pip install dmint
dmint demo               # Optional: run the 7-scenario live red-team simulator in 600ms
dmint init --harness all # Provision .dmint/ keys, per-harness policies, and PreToolUse hooks
dmint doctor             # Verify keys, policies, hooks, and 4 security vectors
```

Test how your generated `policy.json` evaluates commands right from the terminal:

```bash
dmint check -t shell.execute -r "git status"           # -> ALLOW (exit 0)
dmint check -t shell.execute -r "git push origin main" # -> APPROVAL_REQUIRED (exit 1)
dmint check -t shell.execute -r "rm -rf /"             # -> DENY (exit 2)
```

---

## 10-Line Python SDK Example

Protect a Python function with deterministic policy evaluation and single-use human approval using `Dmint.local()` (which automatically initializes `.dmint/` keys and local SQLite storage):

```python
from dmint import ApprovalRequiredError, Dmint, Policy, Rule

# 1. Define deterministic rules (default-deny)
policy = Policy([
    Rule.allow("database", "query"),
    Rule.approval_required("database", "delete"),
])

# 2. Initialize zero-config local engine (.dmint/ keys + SQLite store)
dmint = Dmint.local(policy)

# 3. Guard the callable
@dmint.protect("database.delete")
def delete_records(table: str, condition: str) -> int:
    return 42

# 4. Execution halts and persists a tamper-evident pending approval record
try:
    delete_records("users", "inactive = true")
except ApprovalRequiredError as exc:
    print(f"Intercepted: {exc.code} (Approval ID: {exc.approval_id})")
```

Output:
```text
Intercepted: DMT_APPROVAL_REQUIRED (Approval ID: apr_9k2L...m4P1)
```

The tool was never called. To approve and execute once:
1. Run `dmint approve apr_9k2L...m4P1` in your terminal (or approve in `dmint dashboard`).
2. Call `dmint.retry(delete_records, "users", "inactive = true")`. Dmint verifies the Ed25519 signature against the exact RFC 8785 argument hash, atomically consumes the approval (`APPROVED -> CONSUMED`), and runs the function once.

---

## How It Works

```text
   AI Agent Call (Python Function / PreToolUse Hook / MCP Tool)
         │
         ▼
 1. Parameter Canonicalization (RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme)
         │
         ▼
 2. SHA-256 Request Fingerprinting (b"dmint/request-fingerprint/v2\x00")
         │
         ▼
 3. Deterministic Policy Evaluation (Deny-overrides, default-deny)
         │
 ┌───────┴────────────────────────┐
 │                                │
 ▼                                ▼
ALLOW                     APPROVAL_REQUIRED
 │                                │
Executes Callable          Halts execution; persists record in SQLite/Postgres;
                           emits webhook notification (Slack/Discord/Teams)
                                  │
                                  ▼
                           Human Review (CLI `dmint approve` or Web Dashboard)
                                  │
                                  ▼
                           Ed25519 Assertion Signed & Bound to Exact Arguments
                                  │
                                  ▼
                           Atomic Single-Use Consumption (`APPROVED -> CONSUMED`)
```

---

## Who It Is For (and When to Use Alternatives)

| Your Use Case | Best Tool | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Need self-hosted, Ed25519-signed, single-use human sign-off on sensitive actions in Python, MCP, or coding-agent hooks** | **Dmint** | Approvals are cryptographically bound to the exact RFC 8785 call arguments, usable once, and automatically voided if policy changes. |
| Running entirely on AWS Bedrock AgentCore | AWS AgentCore Policy | Managed Cedar policy enforcement at the AWS gateway. |
| Polyglot enterprise governance across Go, .NET, Java, and Rust | Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit / Cerbos | Broad multi-language SDKs and centralized PDP infrastructure. |
| Content moderation, PII redaction, or prompt-injection classification | LLM Guardrails (Llama Guard, NeMo) | Dmint is a deterministic capability/argument gate, not a text classifier. |

# 5-Minute Quickstart

This guide shows two ways to start using Dmint immediately:
1. **Track A (CLI & Coding Agents)**: Protect shell and file tools in Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI, OpenCode, Cursor, Windsurf, or Cline with `dmint init`.
2. **Track B (Python SDK)**: Protect Python functions with `Dmint.local()`, approve a paused call via `dmint approve`, and execute a single-use retry.

---

## Prerequisites

- **Python**: 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, or 3.13.
- **Operating system**: Linux, macOS, or Windows WSL.

```bash
mkdir dmint-quickstart && cd dmint-quickstart
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install dmint
dmint --version
```

```text
dmint 2.0.4
```

---

## Track A: Coding Agent Hooks in 30 Seconds (`dmint init`)

Run `dmint init` to generate local signing/integrity keys (`.dmint/`), a starter `policy.json` (`shell` and `filesystem` templates), and pre-tool execution hooks for your coding agents:

```bash
dmint init --harness all
dmint doctor
```

Test how your policy evaluates commands from the terminal using `dmint check`:

```bash
# 1. Allowed command (exit code 0)
dmint check --tool shell.execute --resource "git status"

# 2. Approval-required command (exit code 1)
dmint check --tool shell.execute --resource "git push origin main"

# 3. Denied command (exit code 2)
dmint check --tool shell.execute --resource "rm -rf /"
```

When your coding agent triggers an `APPROVAL_REQUIRED` command, approve it from your terminal and tell the agent to retry:

```bash
dmint pending
dmint approve apr_... --by alice@company.com

# Inspect and verify the SHA-256 hash-chained audit log:
dmint logs
dmint logs --verify
```

---

## Track B: Python SDK Quickstart (`Dmint.local`)

### Step 1: Create `policy.json`

```json title="policy.json"
{
  "rules": [
    {
      "effect": "allow",
      "tool": "ledger",
      "action": "view_balance"
    },
    {
      "effect": "approval_required",
      "tool": "ledger",
      "action": "transfer_funds"
    },
    {
      "effect": "deny",
      "tool": "ledger",
      "action": "delete_account"
    }
  ]
}
```

Validate it offline:

```bash
dmint verify-policy policy.json
```

```text
✓ Verified policy.json: 3 rule(s)
  [ALLOW] tool='ledger', action='view_balance', resource='NoResource'
  [APPROVAL_REQUIRED] tool='ledger', action='transfer_funds', resource='NoResource'
  [DENY] tool='ledger', action='delete_account', resource='NoResource'
```

---

### Step 2: Protect Functions in `app.py`

`Dmint.local("policy.json")` automatically provisions `.dmint/signing.key`, `.dmint/integrity.key`, and `.dmint/approvals.sqlite3` with zero boilerplate:

```python title="app.py"
import sys
from dmint import ApprovalRequiredError, AuthorizationError, Dmint

dmint = Dmint.local("policy.json", agent_id="ledger-agent-01")


@dmint.protect("ledger.view_balance")
def view_balance(account_id: str) -> dict:
    return {"account_id": account_id, "balance_usd": 12500}


@dmint.protect("ledger.transfer_funds")
def transfer_funds(from_acct: str, to_acct: str, amount: int) -> dict:
    return {"from": from_acct, "to": to_acct, "amount": amount, "status": "transferred"}


@dmint.protect("ledger.delete_account")
def delete_account(account_id: str) -> dict:
    return {"deleted": account_id}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) > 1 and sys.argv[1] == "--retry":
        # Automatically verifies and consumes the single-use approval from .dmint/approvals.sqlite3
        res = dmint.retry(transfer_funds, "acct_100", "acct_200", 500)
        print(f"[✓] Approved retry succeeded: {res}")
        sys.exit(0)

    # 1. ALLOW: executes immediately
    print("[✓] Balance:", view_balance("acct_100"))

    # 2. DENY: fails closed immediately
    try:
        delete_account("acct_100")
    except AuthorizationError as exc:
        print(f"[✗] Denied as expected: {exc.code}")

    # 3. APPROVAL_REQUIRED: pauses and writes pending record to .dmint/approvals.sqlite3
    try:
        transfer_funds("acct_100", "acct_200", 500)
    except ApprovalRequiredError as exc:
        print(f"[⏸] Paused for approval: {exc.approval_id}")
        print(f"    Run: dmint approve {exc.approval_id}")
        print("    Then run: python app.py --retry")
```

---

### Step 3: Run, Approve, and Retry

1. Run `app.py`:
   ```bash
   python app.py
   ```
   ```text
   [✓] Balance: {'account_id': 'acct_100', 'balance_usd': 12500}
   [✗] Denied as expected: DMT_POLICY_DENIED
   [⏸] Paused for approval: apr_7x9K...
       Run: dmint approve apr_7x9K...
       Then run: python app.py --retry
   ```

2. Approve the pending request in your terminal:
   ```bash
   dmint approve apr_7x9K... --by finance@company.com --reason "Verified invoice #402"
   ```
   ```text
   ✓ Approved 'apr_7x9K...' (ledger.transfer_funds) successfully.
     Reason: Verified invoice #402
   ```

3. Run the approved retry:
   ```bash
   python app.py --retry
   ```
   ```text
   [✓] Approved retry succeeded: {'from': 'acct_100', 'to': 'acct_200', 'amount': 500, 'status': 'transferred'}
   ```

4. Try replaying the exact same retry a second time:
   ```bash
   python app.py --retry
   ```
   It fails closed with `DMT_APPROVAL_CONSUMED` because every Dmint approval assertion is single-use.

DOCUMENT: Protect a Tool End-to-End
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/tutorials/protect-a-tool
SECTION: Tutorials
SUMMARY: Build a complete customer refund service where small refunds execute automatically and larger refunds require a human-approved, single-use credential.
================================================================================

# Tutorial: Require Approval for Sensitive Actions

In this tutorial you will build a customer-support refund service with two deterministic outcomes:

1. Refunds below **$100.00** execute automatically.
2. Refunds from **$100.00 through $500.00** stop and require human approval.
3. The approved host retries the exact same call with a single-use Ed25519 assertion.

The example uses two distinct capabilities so the policy remains deterministic. Dmint does not use “first matching rule” or an `else` branch: a failed constraint is a deny, not a fallthrough. The trusted host code chooses the capability based on the refund amount.

---

## 1. Prerequisites

Create a workspace and install Dmint:

```bash
mkdir dmint-refund-tutorial && cd dmint-refund-tutorial
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install dmint
```

Generate the signing key and storage-integrity key:

```bash
dmint init-keys
```

The default key paths are:

```text
~/.config/dmint/signing.key
~/.config/dmint/integrity.key
```

The command also prints the public key and issuer ID. Copy the `public_key_hex` value; the host verifier needs it. The private key stays with the approval process.

---

## 2. Define the Policy

Create `policy.json`:

```json title="policy.json"
{
  "rules": [
    {
      "effect": "allow",
      "tool": "billing",
      "action": "issue_small_refund",
      "constraints": {
        "properties": {
          "amount": {
            "type": "number",
            "maximum": 99.99
          }
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "effect": "approval_required",
      "tool": "billing",
      "action": "issue_large_refund",
      "constraints": {
        "properties": {
          "amount": {
            "type": "number",
            "minimum": 100,
            "maximum": 500
          }
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Validate it:

```bash
dmint verify-policy policy.json
```

```text
✓ Verified policy.json: 2 rule(s)
  [ALLOW] tool='billing', action='issue_small_refund', resource='NoResource'
  [APPROVAL_REQUIRED] tool='billing', action='issue_large_refund', resource='NoResource'
```

Both rules omit `resource`, which means they match requests with **no resource**. That is intentional for this example, because the capability itself identifies the operation. If you add resource-bearing calls, use an explicit resource selector (and `"resource": "*"` for a global rule).

No catch-all `deny` rule is needed. A request that matches no rule is denied by default with `DMT_DEFAULT_DENIED`.

Record the policy digest:

```bash
dmint policy-digest policy.json
```

---

## 3. Protect the Host Functions

<Tip>
**Fastest Local Setup (`Dmint.local`)**: If your agent and CLI run on the same development machine, you can skip `dmint init-keys` and replace the boilerplate setup below with a single line: `dmint = Dmint.local("policy.json", agent_id="support-agent-01")`. You can then retry with `dmint.retry(issue_large_refund, "cust_42", 250.0, "ticket-1204")` without passing `approval_credential`. The explicit setup below demonstrates the full split-key architecture for multi-host production deployments.
</Tip>

Create `app.py`. Replace `PASTE_PUBLIC_KEY_HEX` with the value printed by `dmint init-keys`.

```python title="app.py"
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from pathlib import Path
import sys

from dmint import (
    ApprovalRequiredError,
    AuthorizationError,
    ApprovalVerifier,
    Dmint,
    Policy,
    PolicyProvenance,
    SQLiteApprovalStore,
    TrustedContext,
    policy_digest,
)
from dmint.core import public_key_from_hex

PUBLIC_KEY_HEX = "PASTE_PUBLIC_KEY_HEX"

policy = Policy.from_file("policy.json")
store = SQLiteApprovalStore("approvals.sqlite3", deployment_epoch="default")

provenance = PolicyProvenance(
    version_id="refund-policy-v1",
    policy_digest=policy_digest(policy),
    evaluated_at=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
)

verifier = ApprovalVerifier(
    trusted_issuers={
        "dmint-authority": public_key_from_hex(PUBLIC_KEY_HEX),
    },
    audience="dmint/dashboard/v1",
)

dmint = Dmint(
    policy=policy,
    agent_id="support-agent-01",
    context=TrustedContext({"tenant": "prod-us"}),
    approval_store=store,
    approval_verifier=verifier,
    policy_provenance=provenance,
    approval_ttl=timedelta(minutes=5),
)

@dmint.protect("billing.issue_small_refund")
def issue_small_refund(customer_id: str, amount: float, reason: str) -> str:
    return f"Refunded ${amount:.2f} to {customer_id}"

@dmint.protect("billing.issue_large_refund")
def issue_large_refund(customer_id: str, amount: float, reason: str) -> str:
    return f"Refunded ${amount:.2f} to {customer_id}"

def issue_refund(customer_id: str, amount: float, reason: str) -> str:
    """Trusted host routing. The agent supplies data, not the route."""
    if amount < 100:
        return issue_small_refund(customer_id, amount, reason)
    if amount <= 500:
        return issue_large_refund(customer_id, amount, reason)
    raise ValueError("Refunds over $500 require manual finance review")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) == 2:
        credential = Path(sys.argv[1]).read_bytes()
        print(
            dmint.retry(
                issue_large_refund,
                "cust_42",
                250.0,
                "ticket-1204",
                approval_credential=credential,
            )
        )
    else:
        print(issue_refund("cust_42", 45.0, "duplicate charge"))
        try:
            print(issue_refund("cust_42", 250.0, "ticket-1204"))
        except ApprovalRequiredError as exc:
            print(f"Approval required: {exc.approval_id}")
```

The `issue_refund` routing function is deliberately trusted host code. An agent cannot select `issue_large_refund` directly to bypass the policy, and the policy’s constraint on `issue_large_refund` denies any out-of-range amount even if a caller uses the capability directly.

---

## 4. Run the First Call

```bash
python app.py
```

The small refund executes. The large refund persists a pending record and does not execute:

```text
Refunded $45.00 to cust_42
Approval required: apr_...
```

The pending record is bound to the full request envelope, including the tool, action, principal, arguments, trusted context, policy version, and policy digest.

---

## 5. Review and Approve

List pending requests:

```bash
dmint pending --db-path approvals.sqlite3
```

```text
APPROVAL ID                                      TOOL/ACTION            RESOURCE/TARGET  PRINCIPAL         REQUESTED
-----------------------------------------------  ---------------------  ---------------  ----------------  ---------
apr_...                                          billing.issue_large_refund  (none)       support-agent-01  0s ago
```

Approve the exact request and write the retry credential:

```bash
dmint approve apr_... \
  --db-path approvals.sqlite3 \
  --policy policy.json \
  --approver-id alice@example.com \
  --authority-issuer dmint-authority \
  --reason "Verified outage ticket #1204" \
  --output-assertion approval.json
```

```text
✓ Approved 'apr_...' (billing.issue_large_refund) successfully.
  Reason: Verified outage ticket #1204
```

The command does **not** execute the refund. It transitions the record to `APPROVED` and writes the signed assertion to `approval.json`. The private key never goes to the agent process.

> The issuer passed to `--authority-issuer` must match the issuer ID in the verifier’s `trusted_issuers` mapping. This example uses `dmint-authority`, the ID printed by `init-keys`.

---

## 6. Retry the Exact Request

Run the host again with the assertion bytes:

```bash
python app.py approval.json
```

```text
Refunded $250.00 to cust_42
```

Dmint verifies the Ed25519 signature, re-evaluates the current policy, binds the assertion to the exact request, and atomically marks the approval `CONSUMED` before executing the function.

Replay the same assertion:

```bash
python app.py approval.json
```

It fails closed with `ApprovalConsumedError` (`DMT_APPROVAL_CONSUMED`). Requesting a different amount or argument also fails with `DMT_APPROVAL_REQUEST_MISMATCH`; an approval for `$250` cannot authorize `$251`.

---

## 7. Use the Dashboard Instead of the CLI

Start the dashboard against the same database:

```bash
dmint dashboard \
  --db-path approvals.sqlite3 \
  --approver-id alice@example.com \
  --authority-issuer dmint-authority \
  --port 8080
```

After login, review the pending request and click **Approve**. The detail page now exposes a **Download assertion artifact** button for approved records. Provide that file to the host:

```bash
python app.py ./apr_....assertion.json
```

The dashboard identity is clearly marked as **self-asserted** unless you configure a trusted reverse-proxy identity header (`DMINT_DASHBOARD_IDENTITY_HEADER` plus `--trusted-proxy`). See [Human Approvals](/guides/human-approvals) for the attribution rules.

---

## 8. What Just Happened

| Event | Result |
|---|---|
| `billing.issue_small_refund` with `$45` | `ALLOW`; function ran |
| `billing.issue_large_refund` with `$250` | `APPROVAL_REQUIRED`; no function execution |
| Approval for `$250` | `APPROVED` record plus signed assertion |
| Retry with the same arguments | Signature/fingerprint verified, record consumed once, function ran |
| Retry with different arguments | `DMT_APPROVAL_REQUEST_MISMATCH`; no execution |
| Replay after success | `DMT_APPROVAL_CONSUMED`; no execution |
| Policy changed after approval | `DMT_APPROVAL_POLICY_INVALID`; approval invalidated |

The request fingerprint is a SHA-256 digest of the **full request envelope**, not “arguments only.” It covers tool, action, principal, integration/capability, resource, trusted context, protocol versions, and arguments.

================================================================================
DOCUMENT: How Dmint Works
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/concepts/how-dmint-works
SECTION: Core Concepts
SUMMARY: The request execution boundary, the deterministic decision engine, and the cryptographic verification lifecycle.
================================================================================

# How Dmint Works

Dmint is an in-process and network-level authorization gate that evaluates AI agent tool calls against deterministic policy rules before execution.

---

## The Core Concept

When an AI agent chooses to call a tool, Dmint intercepts the call, canonicalizes its arguments using RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS), hashes the result into a SHA-256 fingerprint, and evaluates the request against pure boolean rules.

The result is strictly one of three states:

| Decision | Runtime Behavior | Tool Execution Status |
|---|---|---|
| `ALLOW` | The request matches an explicit allow rule and satisfies all parameter constraints. | **Executes immediately**. |
| `DENY` | The request matches a deny rule, or fails to match any allow rule (default-deny). | **Blocked**. Callable is never invoked. Raises `AuthorizationError`. |
| `APPROVAL_REQUIRED` | The request matches a human-review rule. | **Halted**. Execution stops; request parameters are fingerprinted and written to persistent storage. Raises `ApprovalRequiredError`. |

There are no probabilistic decisions, confidence thresholds, or model calls in the runtime decision loop.

---

## The Call Flow

```text
               AI Agent / Tool-Calling Loop
                           │
                           │ 1. Invocation (tool, action, arguments, context)
                           ▼
             ┌───────────────────────────┐
             │  Dmint Enforcement Gate   │
             └─────────────┬─────────────┘
                           │
                           │ 2. Parameter Canonicalization (RFC 8785 JCS)
                           │ 3. SHA-256 Request Fingerprint
                           │ 4. Deterministic Policy Evaluation
                           ▼
               ┌───────────────────────┐
               │  Three Decisions Only │
               └───────────┬───────────┘
         ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
         ▼                 ▼                 ▼
     [ ALLOW ]    [ APPROVAL_REQUIRED ]   [ DENY ]
         │                 │                 │
         │                 │ Persist pending │ Execution blocked;
         │                 │ record & emit   │ raises AuthorizationError
         │                 │ webhook alert   │ (Tool never called)
         │                 ▼                 ▼
         │        ┌─────────────────┐
         │        │ Approval Store  │ (SQLite / PostgreSQL)
         │        └────────┬────────┘
         │                 │
         │                 │ 5. Human Reviews & Signs (Dashboard or CLI)
         │                 ▼
         │        ┌─────────────────┐
         │        │ Signed Ed25519  │
         │        │ Assertion Token │
         │        └────────┬────────┘
         │                 │
         │                 │ 6. Host Retries Tool Call with Approval
         │                 ▼
         │        ┌─────────────────┐
         │        │ Verification    │ - Checks Ed25519 signature
         │        │ & Single-Use    │ - Matches request fingerprint
         │        │ Consumption     │ - Transitions state to CONSUMED
         │        └────────┬────────┘
         │                 │
         └─────────────────┴────────┐
                                    ▼
                         ┌─────────────────────┐
                         │   Protected Tool    │
                         │      Executes       │
                         └─────────────────────┘
```

---

## Detailed Step-by-Step Breakdown

### 1. Interception and Argument Snapshotting
Whether invoked via the `@dmint.protect` Python decorator, a coding-agent `PreToolUse` hook (`dmint hook run`), or the `dmint-mcp` gateway proxy, Dmint captures the exact arguments passed to the tool. Variadic positional (`*args`) and keyword arguments (`**kwargs`) are normalized into a frozen dictionary representation.

### 2. RFC 8785 Canonicalization
JSON serialization is non-deterministic in standard libraries: dictionary keys can be ordered arbitrarily, whitespace varies, and numeric representations can differ. Dmint normalizes all request arguments using RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS):
- Lexicographical sorting of object keys by UTF-16 code units.
- Strict IEEE 754 float representation without trailing zeros or unnecessary exponents.
- Removal of all insignificant whitespace.

### 3. SHA-256 Request Fingerprinting
The canonicalized payload is hashed using SHA-256 with domain separation:
`Domain: b"dmint/request-fingerprint/v2\x00"`

The fingerprint binds:
- Tool namespace and action name (e.g. `ledger.transfer_funds`).
- Calling agent identifier (`agent_id`).
- Integration identifier (`integration_id`).
- Immutable trusted context attributes (e.g. `environment: production`).
- Exact canonical arguments.

### 4. Deterministic Policy Evaluation
The policy engine evaluates rules in strict sequence:
- **Deny-Overrides**: If any matching rule specifies `DENY`, the request is denied immediately.
- **Fail-Closed Default**: If no rule matches, the request is denied.
- **Constraint Validation**: Constraints defined on `ALLOW` rules (such as numerical bounds, string lengths, or regex patterns) must be satisfied. Any constraint failure immediately evaluates to `DENY`.

### 5. Persistent Approval & Notification
When an action requires approval:
- An approval record (`req_...` / `apr_...`) is inserted into SQLite or PostgreSQL in the `PENDING` state.
- If configured, an outgoing webhook notification is asynchronously dispatched to Slack, Discord, or Microsoft Teams with sanitized metadata.

### 6. Human Authorization & Atomic Consumption
When an authorized human reviews and approves the request:
- An Ed25519 digital signature is generated over the approval assertion.
- When the host retries the operation, Dmint executes an atomic transaction (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` in PostgreSQL or immediate transaction in SQLite) that transitions the record to `CONSUMED`.
- If another process attempts to use the same approval token, Dmint rejects it with `DMT_APPROVAL_CONSUMED`.

---

## Performance Characteristics

| Operation | Typical Latency | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| In-Memory Policy Evaluation | **~3 µs** | Pure CPU boolean matching and JCS canonicalization. |
| SQLite Approval Operation | **~2–5 ms** | Disk I/O with WAL mode and row HMAC calculation. |
| PostgreSQL Approval Operation | **~3–8 ms** | Network round-trip and row-level locking transaction. |

---

## What Dmint Does Not Do

- **No Semantic Text Analysis**: Dmint does not scan tool arguments for offensive language or attempt to guess the user's feelings. It enforces structural and cryptographic policies.
- **No In-Process Sandbox Escape Defense**: If an agent running as the same OS user has unrestricted shell access, it can terminate the Python process or edit files directly. Dmint protects the API boundaries it wraps; system-level isolation requires OS containers or dedicated user accounts.

---

## Next Steps

- **[Policy Authoring & Rule Structure](/concepts/policies)**: Explore rule effects, conditions, and argument constraints.
- **[Request Binding & Cryptographic Invariants](/concepts/request-binding)**: Learn how RFC 8785 guarantees byte-level immutability.
- **[Approval Lifecycle](/concepts/approvals)**: Review the 7-state lifecycle machine and replay defenses.


================================================================================
DOCUMENT: Policies and Rules
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/concepts/policies
SECTION: Core Concepts
SUMMARY: Declarative JSON policies, rule effects, deny-overrides precedence, wildcard selectors, context conditions, and argument constraints.
================================================================================

# Policies and Rules

A Dmint **policy** is a static, declarative JSON document that defines which AI-agent tool calls are allowed, denied, or require human approval. The evaluator is deterministic: it never calls an LLM and never learns from traffic.

```text
Policy rule matches?
        │
        ▼
DENY  >  APPROVAL_REQUIRED  >  ALLOW
        │
        └── no rule matches ──► DENY (DMT_DEFAULT_DENIED)
```

---

## Policy Structure

A policy contains an array of `rules`. Every rule has a lowercase `effect`, an exact `tool` selector, an exact `action` selector, and optional scoping fields:

```json title="policy.json"
{
  "rules": [
    {
      "effect": "allow",
      "tool": "database",
      "action": "query",
      "resource": "public.*",
      "resource_kind": "identifier"
    },
    {
      "effect": "approval_required",
      "tool": "database",
      "action": "update",
      "resource": "public.accounts",
      "constraints": {
        "properties": {
          "amount": {
            "type": "number",
            "maximum": 50000
          }
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "effect": "deny",
      "tool": "database",
      "action": "drop",
      "resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
```

Validate the file before deploying it:

```bash
dmint verify-policy policy.json
dmint check -p policy.json -t database.query -r "public.users"
dmint policy-digest policy.json
```

`verify-policy` is offline and deterministic. `policy-digest` prints the domain-separated SHA-256 digest used for policy provenance.

---

## The Three Rule Effects

| Effect | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `allow` | Permit execution if every matching rule’s conditions and constraints pass. |
| `deny` | Reject execution immediately. The protected function never runs. |
| `approval_required` | Persist one pending request and stop. No tool execution occurs until a trusted human approves the exact request. |

Effects are **lowercase only**. `ALLOW`, `APPROVAL_REQUIRED`, and `DENY` are rejected by the loader and `verify-policy`.

All three effects are represented by the runtime enum `Decision.ALLOW`, `Decision.DENY`, and `Decision.APPROVAL_REQUIRED`.

---

## Precedence Is Fixed, Not Sequential

Rules are **not** evaluated first-match-wins. Dmint collects every rule whose selectors, conditions, and constraints match, then applies this fixed precedence:

```text
1. DENY               (highest priority)
2. APPROVAL_REQUIRED
3. ALLOW              (lowest priority)
```

Ordering in the JSON file has no effect. A matching `deny` overrides every matching `approval_required` and `allow`; a matching `approval_required` overrides a matching `allow`.

This is deliberate: a policy author cannot accidentally widen access by placing an `allow` before a `deny`.

If no rule matches, or if a matching rule’s constraint fails, the result is `DENY`:

| Case | Decision | Code |
|---|---|---|
| A `deny` rule matches | `DENY` | `DMT_POLICY_DENIED` |
| No rule matches | `DENY` | `DMT_DEFAULT_DENIED` |
| A matching rule’s constraints fail | `DENY` | `DMT_CONSTRAINT_VIOLATION` |
| A matching `approval_required` rule exists (and no deny wins) | `APPROVAL_REQUIRED` | `DMT_APPROVAL_REQUIRED` |

**Constraint failures do not “fall through” to another rule.** If a request matches an `allow` rule but violates its constraints, Dmint denies the request. To express different handling for different argument ranges, use distinct capabilities (for example `billing.issue_small_refund` and `billing.issue_large_refund`) selected by trusted host code, as the tutorial demonstrates.

---

## Selectors

### `tool` and `action`

- An exact, case-sensitive string matches the request’s `tool` or `action`.
- `"*"` is a whole-field wildcard. It matches any tool or action.
- Partial wildcards such as `"read_*"` are not supported; use exact values or `"*"`.

Wildcard rules participate in the same fixed precedence as exact rules. A wildcard `deny` therefore overrides any more specific `allow`.

### `resource`

The `resource` selector is optional.

| Omitted or `NO_RESOURCE` | `"*"` | Exact string / pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Matches only requests with **no resource** | Matches **any** resource | Matches the request resource according to `resource_kind` |

A global deny or approval rule must use `"resource": "*"`. Writing `Rule.deny("database", "drop")` without a resource does **not** deny resource-bearing calls; it only matches no-resource calls.

Supported `resource_kind` values are `exact`, `path`, `url`, `host`, and `identifier`. The default is derived from the resource value: no-resource for omitted, any for `"*"`, exact for a string. Set `case_sensitive` only where the chosen kind supports it.

### `agent_id`

`agent_id` optionally narrows a rule to one principal. Omit it to match every principal.

### `conditions`

Conditions evaluate only against the host-supplied `TrustedContext`. They never read model output or request arguments.

```json
{
  "effect": "approval_required",
  "tool": "cloud",
  "action": "deploy",
  "conditions": [
    { "field": "environment", "operator": "equals", "value": "production" }
  ]
}
```

Supported operators: `equals`, `notEquals`, `in`, `contains`, `startsWith`, and `endsWith`.

### `constraints`

Constraints validate a rule’s argument values. They can be attached to `allow` and `approval_required` rules; attaching constraints to a `deny` rule is rejected. A matching rule with failing constraints produces `DENY` (`DMT_CONSTRAINT_VIOLATION`) before any effect is applied.

---

## Complete Example

```json title="policy.json"
{
  "rules": [
    {
      "effect": "allow",
      "tool": "filesystem",
      "action": "read_file",
      "resource": "/var/log/*",
      "resource_kind": "path"
    },
    {
      "effect": "approval_required",
      "tool": "database",
      "action": "update",
      "resource": "*",
      "constraints": {
        "properties": {
          "amount": { "type": "number", "maximum": 50000 }
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "effect": "deny",
      "tool": "*",
      "action": "*",
      "resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
```

In this policy the final wildcard `deny` overrides the first two rules for every request. It is a backstop only if it is intended to make the policy deny everything; usually a catch-all deny is omitted because unmatched requests already fail closed. Prefer an explicit deny for the specific dangerous capabilities you want to document.

---

## Policy Provenance

Every pending approval records the policy version and digest that produced the decision. If the policy changes before the request is retried, Dmint rejects the approval with `DMT_APPROVAL_POLICY_INVALID` and invalidates the record. This prevents an approval granted under one policy from authorizing execution under another.

Use `policy-digest` in deployment tooling and pin the value with `expected_policy_digest` when loading a policy from a remote URL.

---

## Verification Checklist

1. Run `dmint verify-policy policy.json` after every edit.
2. Use lowercase effects.
3. Put `"resource": "*"` on any global `deny` or approval rule.
4. Do not rely on rule order.
5. Remember that constraint failure is a deny, not an `else` branch.
6. Keep `policy.json` under version control and rotate its digest deliberately.

---

## Production Policy Templates

Instead of authoring policies from scratch, Dmint provides **7 verified production templates** for common operational domains:
- **`shell`**: Safe terminal commands (`git`, `pytest`, `npm test`) allowed; service management (`systemctl`, `docker`) approval-gated; destructive commands (`rm -rf /`, `dd`, `mkfs`) denied.
- **`filesystem`**: Path-scoped workspace reads allowed; write operations approval-gated; credentials (`.env*`, `*.key`, `*.pem`, `/etc/*`) denied.
- **`postgres`**: `SELECT` and `EXPLAIN` allowed; mutations and DDL approval-gated; `DROP TABLE` and `TRUNCATE` denied.
- **`github`**: Issues and PR reads allowed; PR and issue creation approval-gated; repo deletion and force push denied.
- **`stripe`**: Customer/charge lookups allowed; billing transactions approval-gated; payouts and secret keys denied.
- **`aws`**: Resource inspection allowed; provisioning approval-gated; deletion and termination denied.
- **`kubernetes`**: Pod and log observation allowed; rollouts and scaling approval-gated; cluster deletion denied.

Load templates programmatically via `from dmint.templates import get_template_policy, list_templates`. See the [Policy Templates Reference](/reference/policy-templates) for full JSON schemas and deduplication rules.


================================================================================
DOCUMENT: Exact Request Binding
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/concepts/request-binding
SECTION: Core Concepts
SUMMARY: How RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS) and SHA-256 domain-separated hashing create immutable request fingerprints.
================================================================================

# Exact Request Binding

A critical vulnerability in traditional approval systems is **parameter tampering** or **scope drift**:
- A human operator reviews and approves: `update_account(account_id="acc_99", role="viewer")`
- An adversarial agent modifies the payload before retry: `update_account(account_id="acc_01", role="admin")`

Dmint eliminates this attack vector through **Exact Request Binding**.

An approval in Dmint is never a blanket permission. It is a cryptographic assertion bound strictly to the byte-for-byte canonical hash of one exact request.

---

## The Request Binding Envelope

Before any approval record is created or evaluated, Dmint constructs an immutable request binding envelope:

```json
{
  "action": "transfer_funds",
  "arguments": {
    "account_id": "acc_100",
    "amount": 500.0
  },
  "binding_version": "dmint/request-binding/v2",
  "canonicalization_profile": "dmint/jcs-v2",
  "capability_id": "ledger.transfer_funds",
  "integration_id": "local-runtime",
  "principal_id": "finance-agent-01",
  "resource": {
    "kind": "identifier",
    "value": "accounts"
  },
  "tool": "ledger",
  "trusted_context": {
    "tenant": "prod-us"
  }
}
```

---

## Why RFC 8785 Canonicalization (JCS)?

In standard JSON implementations, semantically identical payloads produce distinct raw string representations:

```json
// Representation A:
{"account_id": "acc_100", "amount": 500.0}

// Representation B (different key order, added spaces, different float formatting):
{  "amount":  500,  "account_id":  "acc_100"  }
```

If hashed naively as raw text, Representation A and Representation B produce completely different SHA-256 hashes, causing false-positive approval mismatches or allowing hash-malleability exploits.

Dmint implements **RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS)**:
1. **UTF-16 Code Unit Key Sorting**: Dictionary keys are sorted lexicographically by their UTF-16 code units (RFC 8785 Section 3.2.3).
2. **Whitespace Stripping**: All whitespace between tokens is removed.
3. **Deterministic Floating-Point Numbers**: Floating-point numbers are formatted using ECMAScript/V8 IEEE 754 string conversion rules without trailing decimal zeros or uppercase exponents.
4. **Surrogate Validation**: Strings containing lone Unicode surrogates are rejected with `CanonicalizationError`.
5. **Depth & Size Limits**: Maximum nesting depth is capped at 100 levels; maximum canonical size is capped at 10 MB.

Under RFC 8785, both Representation A and Representation B serialize to the exact same bytes:
`{"account_id":"acc_100","amount":500}`

---

## SHA-256 Domain Separation

Once the request envelope is serialized to canonical bytes, Dmint computes the SHA-256 request fingerprint:

```python
import hashlib
from dmint.core.canonicalize import canonicalize_bytes

_FINGERPRINT_DOMAIN = b"dmint/request-fingerprint/v2\x00"

canonical_bytes = canonicalize_bytes(request_envelope)
request_fingerprint = hashlib.sha256(_FINGERPRINT_DOMAIN + canonical_bytes).hexdigest()
```

### Why Domain Separation Matters
The prefix `b"dmint/request-fingerprint/v2\x00"` prevents cross-protocol signature forgery. A hash computed for a policy digest (`b"dmint/policy-digest/v1\x00"`) or row integrity check (`b"dmint/approval-record-integrity/v2\x00"`) can never collide with or be substituted for a request fingerprint.

---

## Tampering Scenarios and Fail-Closed Responses

| Attempted Tampering | Attacker Action | Dmint Detection | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Argument Modification** | Changes `amount` from `500` to `5000` | Canonical JCS bytes change; SHA-256 hash mismatch. | Fails closed: `DMT_APPROVAL_REQUEST_MISMATCH` |
| **Agent Spoofing** | Another agent attempts to reuse approved token | `principal_id` mismatch in request envelope. | Fails closed: `DMT_APPROVAL_PRINCIPAL_MISMATCH` |
| **Context Switching** | Replaying approval in `production` that was approved in `staging` | `trusted_context.environment` differs in hash. | Fails closed: `DMT_APPROVAL_REQUEST_MISMATCH` |
| **Policy Modification** | Operator changes policy rules after approval granted | Policy SHA-256 digest changed; epoch invalidated. | Fails closed: `DMT_APPROVAL_POLICY_INVALID` |

---

## Next Steps

- **[Approval Lifecycle & State Machine](/concepts/approvals)**: See how approved assertions transition to single-use `CONSUMED`.
- **[Resource Matching](/concepts/resources)**: How paths, hostnames, and URLs are validated and normalized.


================================================================================
DOCUMENT: Approval Lifecycle and State Machine
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/concepts/approvals
SECTION: Core Concepts
SUMMARY: The 7-state approval lifecycle, Ed25519 digital signatures, atomic single-use consumption, and the retry protocol.
================================================================================

# Approval Lifecycle and State Machine

When an AI agent requests an action governed by an `APPROVAL_REQUIRED` policy rule, Dmint intercepts the call, persists a pending record, and halts execution before the tool is invoked.

Dmint does **not** block or sleep in a polling loop waiting for approval. The protected function raises `ApprovalRequiredError` immediately, allowing the host application to notify the operator and proceed with other work.

---

## The 7-State Lifecycle Machine

An approval record transitions through a strictly validated state machine:

```text
                     ┌───────────┐
                     │  PENDING  │
                     └─────┬─────┘
          ┌────────────────┼────────────────┬────────────────┐
          │                │                │                │
          ▼                ▼                ▼                ▼
    ┌───────────┐    ┌───────────┐    ┌───────────┐    ┌───────────┐
    │ APPROVED  │    │ REJECTED  │    │ CANCELLED │    │  EXPIRED  │
    └─────┬─────┘    └───────────┘    └───────────┘    └───────────┘
          │
          ├────────────────┬────────────────┐
          ▼                ▼                ▼
    ┌───────────┐    ┌───────────┐    ┌────────────────────┐
    │ CONSUMED  │    │  EXPIRED  │    │ POLICY_INVALIDATED │
    └───────────┘    └───────────┘    └────────────────────┘
```

### Complete State Definitions

| State | Trigger | Description | Tool Execution Allowed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PENDING` | Agent initiates call | Request arguments fingerprinted and written to store. | No |
| `APPROVED` | Human signs via UI or CLI | Cryptographic Ed25519 signature generated. | Yes (exactly once on retry) |
| `REJECTED` | Human rejects via UI or CLI | Marked as rejected with optional audit note. | No (fails closed) |
| `CANCELLED` | Host application or agent cancels | Pending request withdrawn before review. | No |
| `EXPIRED` | System clock > `expires_at` | Approval lifetime elapsed (configured via `approval_ttl`, e.g. 5 minutes). | No (`DMT_APPROVAL_EXPIRED`) |
| `POLICY_INVALIDATED`| `policy.json` modified | Policy digest changed, invalidating unconsumed approvals. | No (`DMT_APPROVAL_POLICY_INVALID`) |
| `CONSUMED` | Host retries approved request | Atomically marked consumed as tool executes. | No (subsequent retries fail) |

---

## The End-to-End Retry Protocol

Dmint enforces non-blocking, asynchronous retry semantics:

```text
1. Agent Calls Tool ──► Dmint halts call ──► Returns DMT_APPROVAL_REQUIRED (with req_id, apr_id)
                                                    │
2. Reviewer Inspects Request                        ▼
   (Dashboard / CLI) ──────► dmint approve <apr_id> ──► Signs Ed25519 assertion (Executes NOTHING)
                                                    │
3. Host Retries Call ──────► Dmint Verifier         ▼
                             ├── Checks Ed25519 Signature
                             ├── Verifies Exact Argument Fingerprint
                             ├── Checks TTL & Policy Digest
                             └── Atomically transitions state: APPROVED ──► CONSUMED
                                                    │
4. Protected Tool ◄─────────────────────────────────┘
   Executes ONCE
```

---

## Cryptographic Assertion Format

When approved, `LocalApprovalAuthority` generates an Ed25519 digital signature over the canonical assertion envelope:

```json title="Approval Assertion Envelope"
{
  "algorithm": "Ed25519",
  "credential_version": "dmint/approval-assertion/v2",
  "payload": {
    "approval_id": "apr_01j7v0q9k3...",
    "approver_id": "alice@company.com",
    "approver_kind": "HUMAN",
    "audience": "dmint/dashboard/v1",
    "created_at": "2026-10-16T01:00:00Z",
    "deployment_epoch": "prod-2026",
    "expires_at": "2026-10-16T01:05:00Z",
    "issuer": "dmint-authority",
    "nonce": "n_4x8L0mK...",
    "policy_digest": "sha256:a1b2c3d4...",
    "request_fingerprint": "3b1a8f9024c...",
    "request_id": "req_8v7G9q...",
    "schema_version": "dmint/approval-record/v2"
  },
  "signature": "base64:3f9a..."
}
```

### Security Invariants in the Assertion
- **`request_fingerprint`**: Binds the signature to the exact RFC 8785 canonical arguments.
- **`policy_digest`**: Binds the signature to the active policy epoch.
- **`deployment_epoch`**: Prevents cross-cluster or rollback approval replay.
- **`expires_at`**: Caps validity to a short window (configured via `approval_ttl`, e.g. 5 minutes).

---

## Single-Use Replay Protection

Approvals are single-use tokens. Once executed, the record is permanently marked `CONSUMED`:

### Concurrency Guarantees
- **PostgreSQL**: Dmint uses `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` row-level locks inside a serialized transaction. If 10 concurrent workers receive the same approved assertion and retry simultaneously, exactly one worker acquires the row lock, marks it `CONSUMED`, and runs the tool. The other 9 workers fail closed with `DMT_APPROVAL_CONCURRENT_CONSUME` or `DMT_APPROVAL_CONSUMED`.
- **SQLite**: Dmint uses immediate transactions with `PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000` and thread-safe connection pooling to guarantee atomic serialization.

---

## Row-Level Integrity Protection (HMAC)

To detect out-of-band database tampering (e.g., an unauthorized user editing SQLite with a hex editor or direct SQL to flip `PENDING` to `APPROVED`), every record in the approval store includes an HMAC-SHA256 signature:
`Domain: b"dmint/approval-record-integrity/v2\x00"`

If any database row has been altered without knowledge of the 0600-protected integrity key, Dmint refuses to load or evaluate the row, failing closed with `DMT_APPROVAL_CORRUPT`.

---

## Key Management & Split-Trust Model

How are signing keys managed, and why can't a compromised agent forge an approval?

Dmint operates on a **split-trust model**:
- **The Human Approver** holds the **Ed25519 Private Key** (`private.key`). This file lives strictly on the reviewer's laptop or inside the isolated `dmint-dashboard` service with strict `0600` POSIX permissions. It is never mounted into or accessible by the agent.
- **The Enforcement Gateway** holds only the **Ed25519 Public Key** configured in `trusted_issuers`.

```bash
# 1. Generate the authority keys (Ed25519 private key + HMAC storage key)
dmint init-keys

# 2. Export the public key to configure the gateway
dmint export-public-key --format json
```

When an agent retries an execution, the gateway verifies the Ed25519 signature against its configured `trusted_issuers`. Because the agent has no access to `private.key`, it cannot forge signatures, and replaying old signatures fails because approvals are single-use (`CONSUMED`).

---

## Next Steps

- **[Human Approvals Guide](/guides/human-approvals)**: Step-by-step instructions for reviewing and approving via Dashboard and CLI.
- **[Deployment Model](/operations/deployment-model)**: Process boundaries, user isolation, and key storage permissions.
- **[Error Reference](/reference/errors)**: Meaning and remediation for all `DMT_APPROVAL_*` errors.


================================================================================
DOCUMENT: Resource Matching Engine
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/concepts/resources
SECTION: Core Concepts
SUMMARY: How Dmint normalizes, validates, and matches paths, URLs, hostnames, and identifiers without ReDoS or traversal vulnerabilities.
================================================================================

# Resource Matching Engine

Security policies frequently govern access to specific targets: file paths, database tables, hostnames, or remote endpoints.

In Dmint, resources are categorized by **kind**. Each kind applies deterministic normalization, character validation, and segment-based matching before comparison against policy patterns.

If a resource string is malformed or attempts path traversal, Dmint rejects the request immediately with `DMT_RESOURCE_INVALID` (which deterministically evaluates to `DENY`).

---

## Supported Resource Kinds

| Kind | Purpose | Example Resource | Example Policy Pattern |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | Filesystem paths | `/var/log/app/output.log` | `/var/log/**/*.log` |
| `url` | Remote HTTP/HTTPS endpoints | `https://api.github.com/repos/org/repo` | `https://api.github.com/repos/*/*` |
| `host` | Network hostnames and domains | `db.production.internal` | `*.production.internal` |
| `identifier` | Entity names (tables, queues, users) | `users_v2` | `users_*` |
| `exact` | Commands and opaque strings | `docker ps -a` | `docker *`, `* | sh`, or literal `git status` |

---

## 1. Path Normalization (`kind: "path"`)

String-based path matching is vulnerable to canonicalization discrepancies and directory traversal attacks (`../`). Dmint's path engine enforces strict normalization before matching:

### Normalization Rules
1. **NFC Unicode Normalization**: Converts decomposed characters into canonical precomposed form.
2. **Separator Normalization**: Resolves duplicate slashes (`//` $\to$ `/`), `./` segments, and trailing slashes.
3. **Traversal Resolution**: Resolves relative `../` segments within bounds.

### Hard Rejections (Fail-Closed)
- **Root Escapes**: Paths attempting to traverse above the root directory (e.g. `/var/../../etc/passwd`) are rejected with `DMT_RESOURCE_INVALID`.
- **NUL Bytes (`\0`)**: Immediately rejected.
- **Percent-Encoded Traversal**: Tokens such as `%2f` (`/`) and `%2e%2e` (`..`) are rejected.
- **Backslashes (`\`)**: Rejected in POSIX path mode.

### Wildcard Matching
- `*`: Matches within a single path segment (never crosses `/`).
- `**`: Matches across multiple path segments.
- Matching uses a deterministic segment tokenizer with zero regular expressions, completely immune to ReDoS backtracking.

<Warning>
**Symlink Resolution Responsibility**: String-based path normalization cannot inspect the host filesystem. Resolving symbolic links (e.g. via `os.path.realpath()`) is the tool resolver's responsibility before passing the resolved path to Dmint.
</Warning>

---

## 2. URL and Host Normalization (`kind: "url"`, `"host"`)

Remote endpoints are normalized to prevent server-side request forgery (SSRF) and domain-evasion attacks:

### Normalization Rules
1. **Scheme Validation**: Fails closed if the scheme is not explicitly `http` or `https`. Schemes like `file://`, `ftp://`, or `gopher://` are rejected.
2. **Punycode Conversion**: Internationalized domain names (IDN) with non-ASCII characters are converted to Punycode (`xn--...`).
3. **Trailing-Dot Removal**: Normalizes `example.com.` to `example.com`. Repeated trailing dots (e.g. `example.com..`) are strictly rejected.
4. **Default Port Stripping**: Removes `:80` for HTTP and `:443` for HTTPS.
5. **Userinfo Stripping/Rejection**: URLs containing credentials (e.g. `https://user:pass@evil.com`) are rejected to prevent authority confusion.
6. **Traversal Defense**: URL paths containing `%2f` or `%2e%2e` are rejected.

### Wildcard Semantics
- Domain wildcards (`*.example.com`) strictly match subdomains (e.g. `api.example.com`, `auth.example.com`).
- Path wildcards follow segment-based matching rules.

---

## 3. Identifiers (`kind: "identifier"`)

Used for database tables, topic names, queue names, and user identifiers:
- Leading and trailing whitespace is rejected.
- NUL bytes and control characters are rejected.
- Wildcards (`*`) match strictly alphanumeric and standard identifier characters (`[A-Za-z0-9_.-]*`).

---

## Defining Resources in Code

When protecting Python callables, specify a resource extractor:

```python
# Fixed resource (via callable resolver):
@dmint.protect("database.query", resource=lambda _: "public.users")
def query_users(): ...

# Dynamic resource extracted from arguments:
@dmint.protect(
    "fs.read_file",
    resource=lambda args: args["filepath"],  # Extracted from arguments
)
def read_file(filepath: str) -> str: ...
```

---

## Next Steps

- **[Policy Authoring Guide](/guides/authoring-policies)**: Learn how to author policies with path and domain wildcards.
- **[MCP Gateway SSRF Defenses](/guides/protecting-mcp)**: Review connection-level IP pinning and private network blocking.


================================================================================
DOCUMENT: Protecting Coding-Agent Hooks
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/guides/coding-agent-hooks
SECTION: How-To Guides
SUMMARY: How Dmint intercepts built-in shell, filesystem, planning, and MCP tools in Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI, OpenCode, Cursor, Windsurf, and Cline using dedicated per-harness policy files.
================================================================================

# Protecting Coding-Agent Hooks (`dmint hook`)

Modern AI coding agents execute their highest-impact operations—such as `Bash` / `run_commands`, file edits (`Write`, `Edit`, `apply_patch`, `pre_write_code`), file reads (`Read`, `read_files`, `pre_read_code`), and subagent delegation—through **built-in native tools** in addition to external MCP servers.

`dmint hook` places Dmint's deterministic policy evaluator and single-use Ed25519 human approval engine directly into the official pre-execution hook lifecycle of each coding harness, provisioning a **dedicated policy file per harness** (`.dmint/policies/<harness>.policy.json`) tailored to that harness's complete built-in tool inventory.

```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    AI Coding Harness (Local / Container)                │
│  (Claude Code · OpenAI Codex CLI · OpenCode · Cursor · Windsurf · Cline)│
└───────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
                                    │ 1. Official Pre-Tool Hook Event
                                    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                          dmint hook run                                 │
│  • Unpacks harness-specific envelope & de-stringifies JSON params       │
│  • Inspects all batch items (multi-file apply_patch / run_commands)     │
│  • Evaluates .dmint/policies/<harness>.policy.json (native + canonical) │
│  • Enforces strict precedence: DENY > APPROVAL_REQUIRED > ALLOW         │
└───────────┬───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┬─────────────┘
            │                       │                       │
            ▼                       ▼                       ▼
        [ ALLOW ]          [ APPROVAL_REQUIRED ]        [ DENY ]
            │                       │                       │
     Exit 0 ("allow")        Persists PENDING apr_...   Exit 2 ("deny")
     Tool executes           or consumes APPROVED       Tool blocked
                             assertion once
```

---

## 1. Supported Harnesses, Official Hook Files & Dedicated Policies

Run `dmint init --harness all` (or `dmint hook install --harness <name>`) to configure any or all supported harnesses. Each harness is wired to its own dedicated policy file in `.dmint/policies/<harness>.policy.json`:

| Harness | Flag Value | Generated Hook Configuration File(s) | Dedicated Policy File | Official Hook Mechanism & Output Schema |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Claude Code** | `claude-code` | `.claude/settings.json` | `.dmint/policies/claude-code.policy.json` | `hooks.PreToolUse` (`matcher: "*"`) returning `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision` (`"allow"` \| `"deny"` \| `"ask"`) |
| **OpenAI Codex CLI** | `codex` | `.codex/hooks.json` & `.codex/dmint-hook.sh` | `.dmint/policies/codex.policy.json` | `hooks.PreToolUse` (`matcher: "Bash\|apply_patch\|mcp__.*"`) returning `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision` (`"allow"` \| `"deny"`) + exit `2` on block |
| **OpenCode** | `opencode` | `.opencode/plugins/dmint-guard.ts` & `.opencode/plugin/dmint-guard.ts` | `.dmint/policies/opencode.policy.json` | Native TypeScript plugin hooking `tool.execute.before` (`input.tool`, `output.args`) |
| **Cursor** | `cursor` | `.cursor/hooks.json` (`"version": 1`) | `.dmint/policies/cursor.policy.json` | `preToolUse`, `beforeShellExecution`, `beforeReadFile`, `beforeMCPExecution`, `subagentStart` (`failClosed: true`) returning `{"permission": "allow" \| "deny"}` |
| **Windsurf Cascade** | `windsurf` | `.windsurf/hooks.json` | `.dmint/policies/windsurf.policy.json` | `pre_run_command`, `pre_read_code`, `pre_write_code`, `pre_mcp_tool_use` (`show_output: true`), blocking via exit code `2` |
| **Cline / Roo Code** | `cline` | `.clinerules/hooks/PreToolUse`, `.cline/hooks/PreToolUse.sh`, `.clinerules/hooks.json` | `.dmint/policies/cline.policy.json` | Executable `PreToolUse` scripts returning `{"cancel": false}` on allow and `{"cancel": true, "errorMessage": "..."}` on block |

---

## 2. Per-Harness Built-In Tool Inventory

Because each coding agent ships with its own internal tools for session planning, user questions, code intelligence, and task completion, sharing a single generic policy across harnesses can accidentally default-deny harmless session tools (such as `TodoWrite` in Claude Code, `update_plan` in Codex, `todowrite` in OpenCode, or `attempt_completion` in Cline).

Dmint ships a dedicated built-in policy template (`src/dmint/templates/data/<harness>.json`) for every harness:

| Harness | Allowed Safe Built-In Tools (`ALLOW`) | Approval-Gated Tools (`APPROVAL_REQUIRED`) | Strictly Blocked Targets (`DENY`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Claude Code** | `Read`, `NotebookRead` (workspace), `Glob`, `Grep`, `LS`, `LSP`, `Agent`, `Task`, `AskUserQuestion`, `EnterPlanMode`, `ExitPlanMode`, `ExitWorktree`, `TaskCreate`, `TaskGet`, `TaskList`, `TaskUpdate`, `TaskStop`, `TodoRead`, `TodoWrite`, `ToolSearch`, `WaitForMcpServers`, `ListMcpResourcesTool`, `ReadMcpResourceTool`, `ListAgents`, `ReportFindings`, `SubagentHandback`, `SendFeedback`, `PushNotification`, `CronCreate`, `CronList`, `CronDelete`, `ScheduleWakeup`, `WebSearch`, safe `Bash`/`PowerShell` (`git status`, `pytest`, `npm test`, `ls`) | `Edit`, `MultiEdit`, `Write`, `NotebookEdit` (workspace), `Skill`, `SlashCommand`, `Workflow`, `EnterWorktree`, `WebFetch`, `Artifact`, `ShareOnboardingGuide`, `RemoteTrigger`, `SendMessage`, `SendUserFile`, mutating `Bash` (`git push *`, `docker *`, `npm install *`, `pip install *`, `curl *`) | Destructive `Bash` (`rm -rf /`, `sudo *`, `mkfs *`, `* \| sh`, `* *.env*`), reading or writing `.env*`, `*.key`, `*.pem`, `.dmint/**`, `.claude/**`, `/etc/**` |
| **OpenAI Codex CLI** | `read_file`, `Read`, `view_image` (workspace), `list_dir`, `grep_files`, `search_files`, `update_plan`, `web_search`, `wait`, `close_agent`, safe `Bash`/`exec_command`/`shell` | `apply_patch`, `Edit`, `Write`, `write_file` (workspace), `spawn_agent`, `send_input`, mutating `Bash`/`exec_command` | Destructive `Bash`/`exec_command`, reading or patching `.env*`, `*.key`, `*.pem`, `.dmint/**`, `.codex/**`, `/etc/**` |
| **OpenCode** | `read` (workspace), `grep`, `glob`, `list`, `lsp`, `todowrite`, `todoread`, `question`, `websearch`, safe `bash` | `edit`, `write`, `apply_patch`, `patch` (workspace), `skill`, `task`, `webfetch`, mutating `bash` | Destructive `bash`, reading or editing `.env*`, `*.key`, `*.pem`, `.dmint/**`, `.opencode/**`, `/etc/**` |
| **Cursor** | `Read`, `beforeReadFile`, `beforeTabFileRead`, `read_file` (workspace), `Grep`, `Glob`, `LS`, `codebase_search`, `grep_search`, `file_search`, `list_dir`, `Task`/`subagentStart` (`explore`, `generalPurpose`), safe `Shell`/`beforeShellExecution` | `Write`, `Edit`, `MultiEdit`, `Delete`, `edit_file`, `write_file`, `delete_file`, `search_replace` (workspace), `subagentStart` (`shell`), `beforeMCPExecution`, mutating `Shell`/`beforeShellExecution` | Destructive `Shell`/`beforeShellExecution`, reading or writing `.env*`, `*.key`, `*.pem`, `.dmint/**`, `.cursor/**`, `/etc/**` |
| **Windsurf Cascade** | `pre_read_code`, `read_file`, `view_file`, `view_code_item` (workspace), `grep_search`, `find_by_name`, `list_dir`, `pre_user_prompt`, safe `pre_run_command` | `pre_write_code`, `write_to_file`, `replace_file_content`, `multi_replace_file_content` (workspace), `pre_mcp_tool_use`, mutating `pre_run_command` | Destructive `pre_run_command`, reading or writing `.env*`, `*.key`, `*.pem`, `.dmint/**`, `.windsurf/**`, `.devin/**`, `/etc/**` |
| **Cline / Roo Code** | `read_files`, `read_file` (workspace), `search_files`, `list_files`, `list_code_definition_names`, `ask_followup_question`, `attempt_completion`, `load_mcp_documentation`, `access_mcp_resource`, safe `run_commands`/`execute_command` | `editor`, `write_to_file`, `replace_in_file`, `apply_patch`, `apply_diff`, `insert_content` (workspace), `new_task`, `switch_mode`, `browser_action`, `use_mcp_tool`, `web_fetch`, `web_search`, mutating `run_commands`/`execute_command` | Destructive `run_commands`/`execute_command`, reading or modifying `.clineignore`, `.clinerules/**`, `.cline/**`, `.env*`, `*.key`, `*.pem`, `.dmint/**`, `/etc/**` |

---

## 3. Multi-Resource & Batch Smuggling Protection

Several harnesses allow an agent to batch multiple file edits or shell commands inside a single tool call:
- **Unified Patches (`apply_patch`)**: Codex CLI, OpenCode (`output.args.patchText`), and Cline embed multiple file headers (`*** Add File: ...`, `*** Update File: ...`, `*** Delete File: ...`, `*** Move to: ...`) in one patch body.
- **Batch File Reads (`read_files`)**: Cline accepts `{"files": [{"path": "src/app.py"}, {"path": ".env"}]}`.
- **Batch Commands (`run_commands`)**: Cline accepts `{"commands": ["git status", "rm -rf /"]}`.

`dmint hook run` extracts **every** target file path or command in the batch, evaluates each against the harness's dedicated policy (checking both the native tool name and the normalized capability), and enforces the strictest decision (**`DENY` > `APPROVAL_REQUIRED` > `ALLOW`**). A denied file or command cannot be smuggled inside an otherwise benign batch call.

---

## 4. Single-Use Human Approvals in Hooks

When a coding agent calls a tool that matches an `approval_required` rule (for example, `git push origin main` or editing `src/main.py`):

1. **First Call Pauses**:
   - `dmint hook run` creates a tamper-evident `PENDING` record (`apr_...`) in `.dmint/approvals.sqlite3`.
   - If Slack, Discord, or Microsoft Teams webhooks are configured (`DMINT_SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL`, etc.), a real-time alert is dispatched.
   - The hook outputs a clear message telling the user/agent how to approve:
     ```text
     Dmint APPROVAL_REQUIRED [apr_8k9P...]: shell.execute on 'git push origin main' requires human sign-off.
     To approve, run: `dmint approve apr_8k9P...` (or use `dmint dashboard`), then retry.
     ```
2. **Human Approves**:
   ```bash
   dmint approve apr_8k9P... --by alice@company.com
   ```
3. **Agent Retries the Exact Tool Call**:
   - When the agent re-runs `git push origin main`, `dmint hook run` computes the RFC 8785 request fingerprint, finds the matching `APPROVED` assertion in `.dmint/approvals.sqlite3`, verifies the Ed25519 signature, atomically transitions the record from `APPROVED` $\to$ `CONSUMED`, and returns `ALLOW`.
   - **Tamper Resistance**: If the agent alters the command to `git push origin main --force`, the fingerprint does not match `apr_8k9P...` and execution is blocked.
   - **Replay Protection**: If the agent tries to run `git push origin main` a second time, the consumed assertion cannot be reused.

---

## 5. Shadow Mode (Dry-Run Rollout) & Policy Learning

Adopting a policy across an existing repository is safer as a three-phase rollout: observe, review, then enforce. Shadow mode evaluates every hook event and writes the decision to `.dmint/audit.jsonl`, but never blocks the tool call. Use it to discover the real tool and resource surface of a harness before turning on enforcement.

### Phase 1: Observe with shadow mode

Set `DMINT_MODE=shadow` in the environment used by the hook process, or pass `--mode shadow` when invoking `dmint hook run` directly:

```bash
export DMINT_MODE=shadow
# The harness continues to call `dmint hook run`; decisions are logged, not enforced.
```

For a manual invocation:

```bash
dmint hook run --harness claude-code --mode shadow < payload.json
```

`dmint hook run` still resolves symlinks, expands batch patches and commands, and evaluates the dedicated harness policy. The difference is that would-be `DENY` and `APPROVAL_REQUIRED` outcomes are recorded with `shadow_would_block: true` and the hook allows the call to proceed.

### Phase 2: Review what would have been blocked

```bash
# Show shadow-mode entries that would have been DENIED:
dmint logs --mode shadow --search DMT_POLICY_DENIED

# Show shadow-mode entries that would have required approval:
dmint logs --mode shadow --search DMT_APPROVAL_REQUIRED

# Show decision, level, shadow-block count, and top-blocked-resource breakdown:
dmint logs --mode shadow --stats

# Cryptographically verify the SHA-256 audit chain:
dmint logs --verify
```

### Phase 3: Learn and verify a least-privilege policy

`dmint learn-policy` reads the observed audit events and emits a starter policy. Safe read-only operations become scoped `ALLOW` rules, mutating operations become `APPROVAL_REQUIRED`, and destructive commands or secret paths are never learned as `ALLOW` (they are emitted as explicit `DENY` rules).

```bash
# Synthesize a candidate policy without touching the active policy.json:
dmint learn-policy --from-logs .dmint/audit.jsonl -o policy.learned.json

# Review the diff, then verify the candidate offline:
diff -u policy.json policy.learned.json
dmint verify-policy policy.learned.json
dmint check -p policy.learned.json -t shell.execute -r "git status"
```

After review, replace `policy.json` (or the harness-specific policy under `.dmint/policies/`) and switch back to enforcement by unsetting `DMINT_MODE` or setting it to `enforce`.


================================================================================
DOCUMENT: Python Decorator Integration
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/guides/python-integration
SECTION: How-To Guides
SUMMARY: How to protect Python functions, async coroutines, class methods, and static methods using the @dmint.protect decorator.
================================================================================

# Python Decorator Integration

The `@dmint.protect` decorator places a deterministic authorization gate directly in front of Python callables.

Dmint intercepts invocations, canonicalizes arguments, verifies policies, and persists pending approval records without altering your business logic.

---

## 1. Supported Callable Types

Dmint supports the following callable types:

- **Synchronous Functions** (`def`)
- **Asynchronous Coroutines** (`async def`)
- **Instance Methods** (methods taking `self`)
- **Class Methods** (`@classmethod`, taking `cls`)
- **Static Methods** (`@staticmethod`)

<Note>
**Generators are not supported**: Python generator functions (`yield`) and asynchronous generators (`yield` in `async def`) cannot be decorated because execution resumes in chunks across multiple caller ticks, violating atomic pre-execution authorization.
</Note>

---

## 2. Zero-Config Local Setup (`Dmint.local`)

For local development and single-host workflows, `Dmint.local()` automatically provisions `.dmint/signing.key` (`0600`), `.dmint/integrity.key` (`0600`), and `.dmint/approvals.sqlite3`:

```python title="local_example.py"
from dmint import ApprovalRequiredError, Dmint, Policy, Rule

policy = Policy([
    Rule.allow("payments", "get_status"),
    Rule.approval_required("payments", "refund"),
])

dmint = Dmint.local(policy, agent_id="agent-01")

@dmint.protect("payments.refund")
def issue_refund(payment_id: str, amount: float) -> dict:
    return {"id": payment_id, "refunded": amount}
```

### Explicit Production Setup (`Dmint`)

For distributed or custom-configured production environments:

```python title="sync_example.py"
from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta
from dmint import (
    Dmint,
    Policy,
    Rule,
    PolicyProvenance,
    SQLiteApprovalStore,
    TrustedContext,
    policy_digest,
)

policy = Policy([
    Rule.allow("payments", "get_status"),
    Rule.approval_required("payments", "refund"),
])

store = SQLiteApprovalStore("approvals.sqlite3", deployment_epoch="default")
provenance = PolicyProvenance("v1", policy_digest(policy), datetime.now(timezone.utc))

dmint = Dmint(
    policy=policy,
    agent_id="agent-01",
    context=TrustedContext({"environment": "production"}),
    approval_store=store,
    policy_provenance=provenance,
    approval_ttl=timedelta(minutes=5),
)

@dmint.protect("payments.get_status")
def get_payment_status(payment_id: str) -> dict:
    return {"id": payment_id, "status": "SETTLED"}

@dmint.protect("payments.refund")
def issue_refund(payment_id: str, amount: float) -> dict:
    return {"id": payment_id, "refunded": amount}
```

---

## 3. Asynchronous (`async def`) Protection

When wrapping an `async def` coroutine, Dmint evaluates authorization before the coroutine begins and returns an awaitable result:

```python title="async_example.py"
import asyncio
from dmint import Dmint, Policy, Rule, TrustedContext, ApprovalRequiredError

policy = Policy([
    Rule.allow("api", "fetch"),
    Rule.approval_required("api", "mutate"),
])

dmint = Dmint(
    policy=policy,
    agent_id="async-worker-01",
    context=TrustedContext({"environment": "staging"}),
)

@dmint.protect("api.mutate")
async def async_database_mutate(record_id: str, payload: dict) -> dict:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)  # Simulated async I/O
    return {"record_id": record_id, "updated": True}


async def main():
    try:
        result = await async_database_mutate("rec_99", {"status": "archived"})
        print(f"Result: {result}")
    except ApprovalRequiredError as exc:
        print(f"Halted: {exc.code} for request {exc.request_id}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

---

## 4. Class Methods, Static Methods, and Instance Methods

Dmint cleanly handles OOP method signatures:

```python title="methods_example.py"
class LedgerService:
    def __init__(self, tenant_id: str):
        self.tenant_id = tenant_id

    # Instance method: Dmint strips 'self' from arguments and scopes action as 'LedgerService.record_entry'
    # (Matched by Rule.allow("ledger", "LedgerService.record_entry") or Rule.allow("ledger", "*"))
    @dmint.protect("ledger.record_entry")
    def record_entry(self, entry_id: str, amount: float) -> str:
        return f"Tenant {self.tenant_id}: Recorded entry {entry_id} for ${amount:.2f}"

    # Class method: Dmint preserves class reference
    @classmethod
    @dmint.protect("ledger.get_version")
    def get_version(cls) -> str:
        return "ledger-v2.1"

    # Static method:
    @staticmethod
    @dmint.protect("ledger.compute_tax")
    def compute_tax(subtotal: float, rate: float) -> float:
        return subtotal * rate
```

---

## 5. Dynamic Resource Resolvers

Policies can match against specific resources (such as file paths, database tables, or target URLs). Use a callable `resource` resolver to extract the resource string dynamically from the function's arguments:

```python
# Resource extracted dynamically from arguments dict:
@dmint.protect(
    "filesystem.read",
    resource=lambda args: args["path"],
)
def read_system_file(path: str) -> str:
    with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        return f.read()

# Dynamic resource with compound formatting:
@dmint.protect(
    "database.table_operation",
    resource=lambda args: f"{args['schema']}.{args['table']}",
)
def run_table_op(schema: str, table: str, query: str):
    ...
```

If the resource resolver returns an invalid type or fails validation, Dmint fails closed with `RequestValidationError`.

---

## 6. Remote Policy Loading and Digest Pinning

In microservices or containerized workers, policies can be loaded directly from a centralized HTTPS endpoint with strict SHA-256 digest pinning:

```python
import os
from dmint import Dmint, TrustedContext

# Remote policy loading requires expected_policy_digest:
dmint = Dmint(
    policy_file="https://internal-security.company.com/policies/billing-v2.json",
    expected_policy_digest=os.environ["DMINT_EXPECTED_POLICY_DIGEST"],
    agent_id="agent-01",
    context=TrustedContext({"env": "prod"}),
)
```

If the remote payload does not match the expected SHA-256 digest, Dmint refuses to start and raises `PolicyError`.

---

## 7. Handling Non-JSON Argument Types (`datetime`, `Decimal`, `UUID`, `Path`)

Because Dmint computes deterministic RFC 8785 (JCS) fingerprints, protected functions accept **JSON-native argument types** (`str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, `None`, `list`, `dict`). Passing non-JSON objects such as `datetime`, `Decimal`, `UUID`, or ` pathlib.Path` fails closed with `CanonicalizationError` (`code="DMT_CANONICALIZATION_ERROR"`).

Convert rich types to canonical strings or numbers at the tool boundary before calling the protected function:

```python
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path
from uuid import UUID

@dmint.protect("audit.write_event")
def write_event(event_id: str, path: str, occurred_at: str) -> dict:
    return {"event_id": event_id, "path": path, "occurred_at": occurred_at}

# Normalize rich Python objects to strings at the call site:
def log_user_event(event_id: UUID, path: Path, occurred_at: datetime) -> dict:
    return write_event(str(event_id), path.as_posix(), occurred_at.isoformat())
```

---
