- **[Human Approvals Guide](/guides/human-approvals)**: How to review pending calls and execute approved retries.
- **[Notifications Guide](/guides/notifications)**: Receive instant webhook alerts in Slack, Discord, or Teams.
- **[Core API Reference](/reference/core-api)**: Complete parameter reference for `Dmint` and `Policy`.


================================================================================
DOCUMENT: Protecting MCP Servers
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/guides/protecting-mcp
SECTION: How-To Guides
SUMMARY: Use dmint-mcp as a deterministic enforcement gateway and proxy for Model Context Protocol tools, with schema pinning, SSRF defenses, and approval retry.
================================================================================

# Protecting MCP Servers with `dmint-mcp`

The **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** lets agents discover and invoke tools over a standard interface. A raw MCP server generally executes whatever the agent asks. `dmint-mcp` inserts a deterministic authorization gate between the agent and every downstream tool call:

```text
┌─────────────────┐
│ AI Client/Agent │  (Cursor, Claude Code, Antigravity, custom MCP client)
└────────┬────────┘
         │ JSON-RPC tools/list, tools/call
         ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│        dmint-mcp Gateway        │
│                                 │
│  ├─ tools/list aggregation      │
│  ├─ tool schema hash pinning    │
│  ├─ SSRF / DNS-rebinding guard  │
│  ├─ deterministic policy gate   │
│  └─ approval verification       │
└────────┬────────────────────────┘
         │ authorized calls only
         ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│ Downstream MCP server(s)        │
└─────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## Supported Transports

1. **`stdio`** — local subprocesses, for example `npx @modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres` or `uvx mcp-server-git`.
2. **`streamable-http`** (`streamable_http` is also accepted) — remote MCP endpoints with TLS, SSRF filtering, optional Bearer auth, and connection-level IP pinning.

Loopback HTTP is accepted only for a local development server. Remote endpoints must use HTTPS.

---

## Step 1: Discover Tools and Author the Policy

Use the interactive authoring command to inspect a downstream server and generate both policy and gateway configuration:

```bash
dmint create-mcp-policy \
  --command npx \
  --args "-y @modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres postgresql://localhost/mydb" \
  --integration-id postgres \
  --output policy.json \
  --config-output mcp_protection.json
```

Review `policy.json` before deployment. Start with explicit `allow` rules for the tools you intend to expose, `approval_required` for sensitive mutations, and `deny` for operations that must never run. Precedence is always **DENY > APPROVAL_REQUIRED > ALLOW**.

A generated `mcp_protection.json` contains the policy path, approval database, and integration/tool bindings:

```json title="mcp_protection.json"
{
  "policy_file": "policy.json",
  "approval_db": "./approvals.sqlite3",
  "approval_ttl": 300,
  "disclosure_mode": "dog",
  "integrations": [
    {
      "integration_id": "postgres",
      "transport": "stdio",
      "connection": {
        "command": "npx",
        "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres", "postgresql://localhost/mydb"]
      },
      "tool_bindings": {
        "query": {
          "tool_name": "query",
          "capability": "postgres.query",
          "discovery": "exposed"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

The policy and approval database are **inside this config**. There are no `dmint-mcp --policy` or `dmint-mcp --db-path` flags.

---

## Disclosure Modes: DOG vs GOD vs CAT

When an AI agent calls a tool that is **denied** or **requires human approval**, how much information should be returned to the model?

In an adversarial setting (e.g. indirect prompt injection), disclosing internal policy rules, policy hashes, or stack fingerprints helps attackers probe and reverse-engineer your security boundary. Dmint provides three distinct disclosure modes configured via `"disclosure_mode"` in `mcp_protection.json`:

| Mode | Name | Verbosity | Internal Fingerprints | Recommended For |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **`dog`** (Default) | Transparent | High | Included (`request_fingerprint`, `approval_id`) | Local development, trusted agent loops, debugging |
| **`cat`** | Balanced | Medium | Omitted (workflow ID only) | Semi-trusted agents, multi-agent pipelines |
| **`god`** | Zero-Knowledge | Minimal | Completely Redacted (`DMT_403`) | Hardened production, untrusted agents, high-risk tools |

```text
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   Disclosure Mode Responses Compared                   │
├─────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Mode    │ Response Payload returned to AI Agent on APPROVAL_REQUIRED    │
├─────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ dog     │ {                                                            │
│         │   "status": "approval_required",                             │
│         │   "code": "DMT_APPROVAL_REQUIRED",                           │
│         │   "request_id": "7b8e1a2f-...",                              │
│         │   "approval_id": "c4d3e2f1-...",                             │
│         │   "request_fingerprint": "a3f5... (sha256 hex)",             │
│         │   "message": "Trusted approval is required for this request."│
│         │ }                                                            │
├─────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ cat     │ Dmint enforcement [DMT_APPROVAL_REQUIRED]: approval requested│
│         │ (workflow 7b8e1a2f-...)                                      │
├─────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ god     │ Dmint enforcement [DMT_403]: access denied                   │
└─────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### 1. DOG Mode (`"disclosure_mode": "dog"`)
Returns a structured JSON document. The AI agent can inspect the exact `approval_id` and `request_id`, pause execution, and present the reviewer with actionable metadata.

### 2. CAT Mode (`"disclosure_mode": "cat"`)
Returns a concise status message with the workflow reference (`request_id`), but omits the cryptographic SHA-256 `request_fingerprint`. This prevents the agent from attempting to tamper with or correlate internal hashes.

### 3. GOD Mode (`"disclosure_mode": "god"`)
Implements total information blackout. Whether an action requires approval, matches an explicit deny rule, or fails closed, the gateway returns:
```text
Dmint enforcement [DMT_403]: access denied
```
The adversarial agent receives zero telemetry about whether the tool exists, whether it is an approval pause or hard deny, or what condition caused the failure.

---

## Step 2: Understand the Protections

### Tool schema hash pinning

Dmint pins the SHA-256 digest of each discovered tool schema. If the downstream schema changes, the gateway fails closed with `DMT_MCP_SCHEMA_MISMATCH` until an operator deliberately re-pins it.

### SSRF and DNS rebinding defense

For remote `streamable-http` integrations the gateway:

- rejects non-HTTP(S) schemes, userinfo, `.internal`/`.local` hosts, trailing-dot hostnames, and empty labels;
- resolves non-loopback hostnames and rejects any DNS answer in loopback, RFC 1918 private, link-local, reserved, multicast, or cloud-metadata ranges;
- canonicalizes IDN/Unicode hostnames to IDNA (punycode) before comparison;
- connects to the validated IP for the lifetime of the transport while preserving the original Host header and TLS SNI;
- refuses to fall back to an unpinned transport if the pinned backend cannot be installed.

An internal company MCP server must be reachable through an approved public/private integration path; an example host such as `api.internal.company.com` is rejected by the guard.

### Duplicate JSON keys

The parser rejects duplicate object keys with `DMT_MCP_PROTOCOL_ERROR`, preventing parser-differential attacks such as `{"id": 1, "id": 2}`.

### Approval retry (Automatic Store-Backed or Explicit Credential)

On `APPROVAL_REQUIRED`, the gateway persists a pending record (`apr_...`) and returns the approval ID. Once a human approves the request via `dmint approve <approval_id>` or the web dashboard, there are **two ways** to retry:

1. **Automatic Store-Backed Retry (Recommended for Cursor, Claude Code & Coding Agents)**:
   Simply ask the agent to retry the exact same tool call with the **exact same arguments**. The gateway automatically looks up the unexpired `APPROVED` assertion matching the request's RFC 8785 fingerprint in the approval store, verifies the Ed25519 signature, atomically transitions the record from `APPROVED` to `CONSUMED`, and forwards the clean call downstream. The LLM never needs to see or copy-paste the cryptographic token.
2. **Explicit In-Band Credential (For Stateless or Remote Orchestrators)**:
   Pass the signed assertion JSON string or object under one of the reserved argument keys (`_dmint_approval`, `dmint_approval`, or `approval_credential`). The gateway strips the reserved key before forwarding arguments downstream and consumes the assertion once.

---

## Step 3: Launch the Gateway

Stdio mode for a desktop client:

```bash
dmint-mcp -c mcp_protection.json
```

Streamable-HTTP mode:

```bash
dmint-mcp \
  -c mcp_protection.json \
  --transport http \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8000 \
  --auth-token "replace-with-a-long-random-token"
```

A non-loopback HTTP bind is refused unless an auth token is configured. Keep the bind on loopback behind a reverse proxy when possible.

Optional policy pinning:

```bash
dmint policy-digest policy.json
dmint-mcp -c mcp_protection.json --expected-policy-digest <sha256-hex>
```

---

## Step 4: Configure the Agent

Point the agent at `dmint-mcp`, not at the downstream server. Example Cursor/Claude Code configuration:

```json title="mcp.json"
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "protected-postgres": {
      "command": "dmint-mcp",
      "args": [
        "-c",
        "/absolute/path/to/mcp_protection.json"
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

For HTTP transport, use the gateway URL and the configured Bearer token in the client’s MCP server settings.

Every `tools/list` and `tools/call` now passes through Dmint’s deterministic policy evaluator. A `DENY` or unresolved `APPROVAL_REQUIRED` never reaches the downstream server.

---

## Notification Dispatch

The MCP gateway dispatches Slack/Discord/Teams notifications when the configured webhook environment variables are present. Dispatch runs in a bounded worker thread, one notification at a time, so a slow webhook does not block the asyncio event loop. Webhook failures are logged and never change the authorization decision. Core (`Dmint`) itself does **not** dispatch webhooks.

---

================================================================================
DOCUMENT: Human Approvals
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/guides/human-approvals
SECTION: How-To Guides
SUMMARY: Review pending requests and transfer a signed, single-use Ed25519 assertion from the dashboard or CLI to the protected host.
================================================================================

# Human Approvals via Dashboard and CLI

When a policy evaluates to `APPROVAL_REQUIRED`, Dmint persists one `PENDING` record and halts. A human reviews the exact request, approves or rejects it, and — if approved — gives the protected host a signed assertion for the retry.

The approval itself does **not** execute the tool. Execution happens only when the host calls `engine.retry(...)` (or MCP retries with an assertion argument) and Core verifies and consumes that assertion.

---

## Approval Lifecycle

```text
APPROVAL_REQUIRED
       │
       ▼
    PENDING ── reject ──► REJECTED
       │
     approve
       │
       ▼
   APPROVED ── download/issue assertion ──► host retry
       │                                      │
       │                                verify + consume
       │                                      │
       │                                      ▼
       │                                   CONSUMED
       └── policy changed / expired ──► POLICY_INVALIDATED / EXPIRED
```

The record is bound to the full request envelope. An approval for arguments `A` cannot be used for arguments `B`; a consumed assertion cannot be replayed.

---

## Method 1: Web Dashboard

The dashboard is a local FastAPI application. It accesses approvals exclusively through `dmint.dashboard.CoreClient` and Core public APIs; it never issues SQL directly.

### Start the dashboard

```bash
dmint dashboard \
  --db-path ./approvals.sqlite3 \
  --approver-id alice@example.com \
  --authority-issuer dmint-authority \
  --port 8080
```

For PostgreSQL:

```bash
dmint dashboard \
  --database-url "postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/dmint" \
  --deployment-epoch production \
  --approver-id alice@example.com \
  --authority-issuer dmint-authority
```

Defaults:

- bind: `127.0.0.1:8080`;
- signing key: `~/.config/dmint/signing.key` (override with `--key-file` or `DMINT_KEY_FILE`);
- authority issuer: `dmint-dashboard` (this example sets `dmint-authority` so the host verifier can use the issuer printed by `dmint init-keys`);
- approval audience: `dmint/dashboard/v1`.

A non-loopback bind is refused unless `--allow-public-bind` is explicit, and it still requires authentication. Prefer loopback behind a reverse proxy.

### Authentication

Set a token inline or from a permission-restricted file:

```bash
export DMINT_DASHBOARD_TOKEN="$(python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))')"
dmint dashboard --db-path ./approvals.sqlite3

# Or:
dmint dashboard --db-path ./approvals.sqlite3 --token-file /etc/dmint/dashboard.token
```

Token files must be mode `0600`. If no token is configured, the dashboard generates a one-time token and prints it in the startup banner. The dashboard also enforces host/origin checks, CSRF tokens, session timeouts, and login rate limiting.

### Approver identity attribution

The dashboard distinguishes three identity sources:

| Source | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **self-asserted** | The label was typed into the login form. It is an audit label, not proof of identity. |
| **trusted_proxy** | The label came from a configured trusted reverse-proxy header. |
| **shared-token** | API access with the shared bearer token; no individual human was authenticated. |

To use a trusted reverse proxy, configure **both** the proxy mode and the header name. Configuring `DMINT_DASHBOARD_IDENTITY_HEADER` without enabling trusted-proxy mode is rejected at startup rather than silently ignored. For example:

```bash
export DMINT_DASHBOARD_TRUSTED_PROXY=1
export DMINT_DASHBOARD_IDENTITY_HEADER=X-Auth-User

dmint dashboard \
  --db-path ./approvals.sqlite3 \
  --trusted-proxy
```

The reverse proxy must strip any client-supplied `X-Auth-User` header and set it from the authenticated session. If the header is configured and missing at login, the dashboard fails the login with `401` and does not create a session. It never falls back to the form value in trusted-proxy mode. If the header disappears from an existing session, approval, rejection, and assertion-download requests fail with `401` instead of being attributed to an unauthenticated label.

The form label is displayed with a **self-asserted** badge. Do not describe it as independently verified identity.

### Review and decide

1. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8080` and sign in.
2. Open the pending approval. The detail page shows tool/action, agent, resource, canonical arguments, timestamps, expiry, and policy provenance.
3. Click **Approve** or **Reject**. Approval records the session identity and transitions `PENDING → APPROVED`.

### Download the retry assertion

After approval, the detail page shows **Download assertion artifact**. The button calls:

```text
GET /approvals/{approval_id}/assertion
```

The endpoint requires an authenticated session, issues a fresh signed assertion for the `APPROVED` record, and returns it as:

```text
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="{approval_id}.assertion.json"
Cache-Control: no-store
```

The artifact is a **single-use credential**. Treat it like a secret: do not place it in prompts, chat logs, agent memory, or dashboards. Download only after approval; a `PENDING` record returns `409` (`assertion_not_available`).

The first assertion created internally during `approve_pending()` is discarded. The download endpoint re-issues a fresh assertion for the same approved record, which avoids exposing a credential in the redirect response.

---

## Method 2: Terminal CLI

### List pending requests

```bash
dmint pending --db-path ./approvals.sqlite3
```

```text
APPROVAL ID       TOOL/ACTION            RESOURCE/TARGET  PRINCIPAL         REQUESTED
----------------  ---------------------  ---------------  ----------------  ---------
apr_...           ledger.transfer_funds  (none)           finance-agent-01  2m ago
```

Use `--database-url` / `DMINT_DATABASE_URL` for PostgreSQL, and `--deployment-epoch` when the store uses a non-default epoch.

### Approve and write the assertion

```bash
dmint approve apr_... \
  --db-path ./approvals.sqlite3 \
  --policy ./policy.json \
  --approver-id alice@example.com \
  --authority-issuer dmint-authority \
  --reason "Verified ticket #1204" \
  --output-assertion ./approval.json
```

```text
✓ Approved 'apr_...' (ledger.transfer_funds) successfully.
  Reason: Verified ticket #1204
```

`--policy` makes the CLI re-verify the current policy file and fail closed if it no longer allows the request. If omitted, the CLI first uses the store’s authoritative policy, then a local `policy.json` if present. `approve` automatically persists the signed Ed25519 assertion inside the approval store so local hosts (`Dmint.local()`, `dmint-mcp`, and `dmint hook run`) can consume it automatically on retry. Pass `--output-assertion ./approval.json` if you also want to export the signed assertion file to a separate host.

The CLI never executes the protected tool. It only transitions the record and optionally writes the assertion.

### Reject

```bash
dmint reject apr_... \
  --db-path ./approvals.sqlite3 \
  --reason "SQL targets an unapproved table"
```

Any retry after rejection fails closed. A rejected approval cannot be “un-rejected”; create and review a new request.

---

## Executing the Approved Retry

### Python host

```python
from pathlib import Path

# Option A: Automatic store lookup (when sharing the same SQLite/Postgres store):
result = engine.retry(transfer_funds, "acc_100", 500.0)

# Option B: Explicit assertion bytes (from --output-assertion or dashboard download):
result = engine.retry(
    transfer_funds,
    "acc_100",
    500.0,
    approval_credential=Path("./approval.json").read_bytes(),
)
```

The callable and keyword/positional arguments must be the same as the original invocation. `engine.retry` verifies the signature and binding, re-evaluates the current policy, atomically consumes the approval, and then executes the function once.

### MCP gateway

Add the assertion under one reserved argument key:

```json
{
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "update_database",
    "arguments": {
      "record_id": 42,
      "action": "archive",
      "_dmint_approval": "<assertion-json-string-or-object>"
    }
  }
}
```

Aliases `dmint_approval` and `approval_credential` are also accepted. The gateway removes the reserved key before forwarding clean arguments downstream.

### Deployment epochs

The runtime and approver must use the same deployment epoch. An assertion issued under one epoch cannot be consumed under another (`DMT_APPROVAL_DEPLOYMENT_INVALID`). Configure this on the engine/store, CLI, dashboard, and MCP gateway consistently.

---

## Failure Semantics

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Approval for `$250`, retry for `$251` | `DMT_APPROVAL_REQUEST_MISMATCH`; no execution |
| Assertion replayed after consumption | `DMT_APPROVAL_CONSUMED`; no execution |
| Policy digest/version changed after approval | `DMT_APPROVAL_POLICY_INVALID`; no execution |
| Record expired | `DMT_APPROVAL_EXPIRED`; create a new request |
| Wrong issuer/public key | `DMT_APPROVAL_ISSUER_INVALID` or `DMT_APPROVAL_SIGNATURE_INVALID` |
| Trusted proxy identity header missing | Login fails closed; no session |
| Download requested for a non-approved record | `409`; no assertion |

---

================================================================================
DOCUMENT: Approval Notifications and Webhooks
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/guides/notifications
SECTION: How-To Guides
SUMMARY: Configure Slack, Discord, and Microsoft Teams alerts for MCP approval and denial events, with DNS-pinned delivery and strict authorization isolation.
================================================================================

# Approval Notifications and Webhooks

The `dmint-mcp` gateway can send an outbound notification when an MCP tool call needs human approval or is explicitly denied. Supported destinations are Slack incoming webhooks, Discord webhooks, and Microsoft Teams connectors.

Notifications are an **integration-layer side effect**. They are not part of the authorization decision, and Core (`Dmint`) does not dispatch them.

---

## Architecture and Guarantees

```text
MCP tool call
     │
     ▼
EnforcementGate (asyncio event loop)
     │  decision: APPROVAL_REQUIRED or DENY
     ├───────────────────────────────┐
     ▼                               ▼
Persist / reject              asyncio.to_thread(...)
(decision is final)                   │
                                      ▼
                              serialized notifier
                              (one dispatch at a time)
                                      │
                         ┌────────────┼────────────┐
                         ▼            ▼            ▼
                      Slack        Discord      Teams
```

<Warning>
**Authorization isolation:** webhook failures, timeouts, HTTP 4xx/5xx responses, malformed URLs, and DNS failures never change the authorization decision and never cause the protected tool to execute. The MCP gateway catches and logs dispatch failures. A slow webhook blocks only that request’s notification handoff; it does not block the event loop, and concurrent dispatches are serialized.
</Warning>

`route_call` awaits the notification handoff before returning the approval/denial response. Dispatch is therefore **at-most-once and synchronous from the caller’s perspective**, not fire-and-forget. There is no automatic retry. If delivery is operationally important, monitor webhook logs and use a separate reliable queue.

---

## Configuration

Set any combination of the following environment variables in the **gateway** process:

| Variable | Destination | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `DMINT_SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL` | Slack | Incoming webhook URL. |
| `DMINT_DISCORD_WEBHOOK_URL` | Discord | Channel webhook URL. |
| `DMINT_TEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL` | Microsoft Teams | Connector URL. |
| `DMINT_MSTEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL` | Microsoft Teams | Legacy alias used only when `DMINT_TEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL` is unset. |
| `DMINT_WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT` | All | Positive request timeout in seconds (default `3.0`). Invalid or non-positive values fall back to the default. |
| `DMINT_WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_HOSTS` | All | Optional comma-separated hostname allowlist. Listed hosts skip the private/metadata address rejection, but still require HTTPS and DNS-pinned delivery. Use only for an operator-controlled internal destination. |

The gateway constructs the notifier from these variables when no `webhook_notifier` was injected. The `dmint dashboard` and Core Python API do not read these variables for authorization purposes.

---

## Payload Content

Approval notifications include:

- approval ID (`apr_...`);
- agent/principal ID;
- tool and action (`tool.action`);
- resource/target, or `(none)`;
- a CLI approval command (`dmint approve apr_...`, with `--deployment-epoch` when non-default);
- the destination-specific formatting for Slack Block Kit, Discord embeds, or Teams MessageCard.

Denial notifications include the tool/action, resource, agent ID, and request ID.

The payload does **not** include raw argument values, a request fingerprint, or the full approval command with database credentials. The CLI command intentionally relies on `DMINT_DATABASE_URL` / local environment configuration rather than embedding a connection string in a chat message.

---

## Security Defenses

### 1. Mention neutralization

Model-generated text can contain Slack/Discord mention syntax. Dmint inserts a zero-width space so injected approval arguments cannot notify a channel:

- `@everyone` → `@\u200beveryone`
- `@here` → `@\u200bhere`
- `<!channel>` → `<!&#8203;channel>` (zero-width inserted after `<!`)
- `<@123456>` / `<@&role>` → neutralized

These transformations apply to the fields that are rendered in notifications.

### 2. Markdown/link neutralization

Markdown link syntax `[label](url)` is rewritten to `[label] (url)`, and Slack-style bracketed URLs are neutralized. This reduces spoofed-link risk in approval messages.

### 3. Length and line bounds

Fields are stripped of carriage returns/newlines and truncated to 256 characters. Resource values and webhook credentials are redacted where applicable.

### 4. DNS pinning and SSRF guard

For every webhook URL Dmint:

1. requires `https://`;
2. rejects userinfo, empty labels, trailing-dot hostnames, and non-public literal addresses;
3. resolves the hostname once and rejects loopback, RFC 1918 private, link-local, reserved, multicast, unspecified, shared-address (`100.64.0.0/10`), and cloud-metadata destinations;
4. connects to the **validated IP** while preserving the original `Host` header and TLS SNI;
5. disables redirects and environment HTTP proxies;
6. rejects invalid or ambiguous webhook URLs with `MCPConfigurationError` before any connection.

The pinned connection removes the DNS-rebinding window between validation and POST. `DMINT_WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_HOSTS` is an explicit operator override for private destinations; it does not disable TLS verification or the no-redirect policy.

---

## Programmatic MCP Usage

Hosts that construct the gateway directly can inject a notifier:

```python
from dmint.core.webhooks import WebhookConfig, WebhookNotifier
from dmint.mcp import MCPGateway

notifier = WebhookNotifier(
    WebhookConfig(
        slack_url="https://hooks.slack.com/services/...",
        timeout=3.0,
    )
)
gateway = MCPGateway(config, webhook_notifier=notifier)
```

Do not pass `webhook_notifier` to `Dmint(...)` expecting Core to dispatch it. That parameter is deprecated and inert: Core emits a `DeprecationWarning`, and the notifier is never invoked. This preserves Core’s zero-network-call authorization invariant.

---

## Failure Behavior

| Failure | Effect on authorization | Effect on notification |
|---|---|---|
| Webhook timeout | None; decision unchanged | Logged warning; no retry |
| HTTP 4xx/5xx | None; decision unchanged | Logged warning; no retry |
| DNS/SSRF rejection | None; decision unchanged | Logged warning; no connection |
| Notification disabled/unconfigured | None | No-op |

If notification delivery is a compliance requirement, run a durable event pipeline outside Dmint based on the persisted approval records; do not make tool execution depend on webhook availability.

---

- [Human Approvals](/guides/human-approvals) — dashboard and CLI review, assertion handoff.
- [Protecting MCP Servers](/guides/protecting-mcp) — gateway setup and approval retry.
- [Approval Lifecycle](/concepts/approvals) — states, expiry, and single-use consumption.


================================================================================
DOCUMENT: Policy Authoring
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/guides/authoring-policies
SECTION: How-To Guides
SUMMARY: How to compile plain-language access requirements into verified, schema-compliant policies using dmint create-policy and create-mcp-policy.
================================================================================

# Authoring Security Policies

Dmint provides command-line wizards to translate natural-language access requirements into verified, schema-compliant `policy.json` and `mcp_protection.json` files.

---

## 1. Four Ways to Create a Policy (`dmint create-policy`)

`dmint create-policy` supports **3 completely offline modes** (zero API keys required) plus **AI-assisted compilation**:

```bash
# Mode A: Built-in Domain Templates (100% Offline — shell, filesystem, postgres, github, stripe, aws, kubernetes)
dmint create-policy --template shell,filesystem,postgres -o policy.json

# Mode B: Inline Rule Flags (100% Offline — repeatable -r <effect>:<tool>.<action>[:<resource>[:<kind>]])
dmint create-policy -r "allow:postgres.select:users" -r "approval_required:stripe.refund:*" -o policy.json

# Mode C: Interactive Terminal Rule Builder (100% Offline step-by-step prompts)
dmint create-policy --interactive -o policy.json

# Mode D: Inline Natural-Language Prompt or Markdown Requirements File (AI-Assisted)
dmint create-policy --prompt "Allow read-only SQL queries, require approval for schema updates" -o policy.json
```

When protecting internal functions or APIs via a markdown file, draft your security requirements in `access.md`:

```markdown title="access.md"
# Database Access Security Requirements

- The agent is permitted to run SELECT queries on any table.
- Inserting or updating records in the 'users' table requires explicit human approval.
- Dropping tables or executing administrative schema changes is strictly denied.
```

Compile `access.md` into `policy.json`:

```bash
dmint create-policy -f access.md -o policy.json -y
```

### Supported Providers and Models

You can specify the LLM provider via `--provider`:

| Provider | Option | Environment Variable | Default Model |
|---|---|---|---|
| **OpenAI** | `--provider openai` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | `gpt-4o-mini` |
| **Gemini** | `--provider gemini` | `GEMINI_API_KEY` | `gemini-1.5-flash` |
| **Groq** | `--provider groq` | `GROQ_API_KEY` | `llama-3.1-70b-versatile` |
| **Custom / Ollama** | `--base-url http://localhost:11434/v1` | `--api-key <KEY>` | Provider-specific |

---

## 2. Authoring for MCP Servers (`dmint create-mcp-policy`)

For Model Context Protocol servers (stdio or streamable HTTP), `dmint create-mcp-policy` connects to the server, queries `tools/list`, and generates both the runtime policy and the gateway configuration:

```bash
dmint create-mcp-policy \
  --command npx \
  --args "-y @modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres postgresql://localhost/mydb" \
  --integration-id postgres \
  -f access.md \
  -o policy.json \
  --config-output mcp_protection.json \
  --non-interactive -y

# Or 100% Offline Auto-Classification (no LLM API key required):
dmint create-mcp-policy \
  --command npx \
  --args "-y @modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres postgresql://localhost/mydb" \
  --integration-id postgres \
  --offline -y
```

---

## 3. Offline Policy Verification (`dmint verify-policy`)

Before deploying any generated policy to production, validate it offline. This step is **completely deterministic and makes zero LLM calls**:

```bash
dmint verify-policy policy.json
```

Output:
```text
✓ Verified policy.json: 3 rule(s)
  [ALLOW] tool='database', action='select', resource='*'
  [APPROVAL_REQUIRED] tool='database', action='update', resource='users'
  [DENY] tool='database', action='drop', resource='*'
```

### Checks Performed by `verify-policy`
- Schema compliance against the official Dmint specification.
- Validation that rule effects are lowercase `allow`, `approval_required`, or `deny`.
- Verification that no constraints are attached to `DENY` rules.
- ReDoS budget limits on regex patterns (max 256 chars, repetition bound).
- Resource string syntax validation.

---

## 4. Policy Digest Pinning (`dmint policy-digest`)

Calculate the SHA-256 digest of your policy file for runtime pinning:

```bash
dmint policy-digest policy.json
```

Output:
```text
6a8b75f28c19a4e3...
```

Export this value as `DMINT_EXPECTED_POLICY_DIGEST` in your deployment environment. If the file is altered on disk, Dmint will refuse to initialize.

---

## Next Steps

- **[Policy Schema Reference](/reference/policy-schema)**: Complete specification of all rule properties and operators.
- **[MCP Protection Schema](/reference/mcp-protection-schema)**: Configuration options for `mcp_protection.json`.

DOCUMENT: AI Coding Agent Skills
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/guides/agent-skills
SECTION: How-To Guides
SUMMARY: How to install the official dmint-policy-manager skill into AI coding assistants like Antigravity, Claude Code, and Cursor.
================================================================================

# AI Coding Agent Skills

When using AI coding assistants (such as Google Antigravity, Gemini CLI, Claude Code, or Cursor), you can install the official **`dmint-policy-manager`** skill.

This equips your AI coding agent with the system prompts, threat models, and authoring guidelines required to create and verify Dmint policies directly in your chat interface.

---

## Installing the Skill (`dmint install-skill`)

Dmint bundles the official skill and provides an installation command:

```bash
# Interactive installation (prompts for destination):
dmint install-skill
```

```text
Dmint AI Coding Agent Skill Installer

Choose installation destination:
  [1] .agents/skills/          (Recommended: Workspace standard for Antigravity, Gemini CLI, Cursor)
  [2] .agent/skills/           (Alternative workspace path)
  [3] ~/.gemini/config/skills/ (Global config for Antigravity / Gemini)
  [4] ~/.claude/skills/        (Global config for Claude Code)
  [5] Type custom path
```

---

## Non-Interactive & Automated Installation

For scripted setups or Docker environments:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Project Workspace (.agents/skills/)">
    ```bash
    dmint install-skill -y
    # Installs to .agents/skills/dmint-policy-manager/
    ```
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Global Gemini / Antigravity">
    ```bash
    dmint install-skill --global
    # Installs to ~/.gemini/config/skills/dmint-policy-manager/
    ```
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Global Claude Code">
    ```bash
    dmint install-skill --claude
    # Installs to ~/.claude/skills/dmint-policy-manager/
    ```
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Custom Directory">
    ```bash
    dmint install-skill --dest ./my-agent-rules/skills
    ```
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

---

## What the Skill Teaches Your AI Agent

Once installed in your project, your AI assistant automatically adheres to these invariants:

1. **Least Privilege Principles**: When drafting policies, the agent defaults unmentioned actions to `DENY`.
2. **Wildcard Containment**: The agent is instructed never to replace specific resources with broad wildcards (`*`) without explicit developer confirmation.
3. **Verification Before Deployment**: The agent will run `dmint verify-policy` to ensure syntactic and semantic validity before committing policy files.
4. **Separation of Concerns**: The agent understands that an LLM can draft policies at development time, but can *never* participate in runtime authorization.

---

## Security Hardening

The `dmint install-skill` command includes strict path sanitization:
- Whitelists skill names against `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$`.
- Rejects path traversal payloads (`../`, `..\\`, absolute root escapes).
- Uses atomic file writes with file descriptor validation to prevent symlink hijacking.


================================================================================
DOCUMENT: Claude Code, Codex & OpenCode Hooks
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/integrations/claude-code
SECTION: Integrations
SUMMARY: How to enforce deterministic policy rules and single-use human approvals on native shell, file, and MCP tools in Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and OpenCode.
================================================================================

# Claude Code, Codex & OpenCode Integration

AI coding agents execute two kinds of tools:
1. **Built-in native tools** (`Bash` / `exec_command`, `Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `MultiEdit`) that run directly inside the agent harness.
2. **Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools** (`mcp__postgres__query`, etc.) that run over stdio or Streamable HTTP.

Dmint protects **both** layers:
- **`dmint hook`** intercepts built-in shell, filesystem, and MCP tool calls via the harness's native `PreToolUse` / `tool.execute.before` hook before a command ever runs.
- **`dmint-mcp`** wraps downstream MCP servers in a fail-closed proxy.

---

## 1. 30-Second Setup (`dmint init`)

In your project directory, run a single command to generate cryptographic keys (`.dmint/`), a starter `policy.json` (covering `shell` and `filesystem` tools), and pre-tool hooks for your coding agent:

```bash
# Install for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Windsurf, and Cline at once:
dmint init --harness all

# Or target a specific harness:
dmint init --harness claude-code
dmint init --harness codex
dmint init --harness opencode
```

What this creates:
- `.dmint/policies/<harness>.policy.json` & `policy.json` — Dedicated per-harness policies covering all built-in tools for Claude Code (`claude-code.policy.json`), Codex (`codex.policy.json`), and OpenCode (`opencode.policy.json`).
- `.dmint/signing.key` & `.dmint/integrity.key` (`0600` permissions) — Ed25519 approval signing key and HMAC store integrity key.
- `.claude/settings.json` — Claude Code `PreToolUse` hook matching `Bash|Read|Write|Edit|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit|WebFetch|mcp__.*`.
- `.codex/hooks.json` & `.codex/dmint-hook.sh` — OpenAI Codex CLI pre-execution hook.
- `.opencode/plugin/dmint-guard.ts` — OpenCode `tool.execute.before` guard plugin.

---

## 2. Test Your Policy from the Terminal (`dmint check`)

Before launching your agent, verify how your `policy.json` evaluates any tool call:

```bash
# Safe inspection command -> ALLOW (exit code 0)
dmint check --tool shell.execute --resource "git status"

# Sensitive command -> APPROVAL_REQUIRED (exit code 1)
dmint check --tool shell.execute --resource "git push origin main"

# Destructive command -> DENY (exit code 2)
dmint check --tool shell.execute --resource "rm -rf /"
```

---

## 3. How the Approval Loop Works in Practice

When Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode attempts an action marked `approval_required` (such as `git push origin main` or `docker run ...`):

1. **Intercept & Pause**: `dmint hook run` halts the tool call, saves a tamper-evident `PENDING` record (`apr_...`) in `.dmint/approvals.sqlite3`, and returns the exact approval command to the agent/user:
   ```text
   Dmint APPROVAL_REQUIRED [apr_9k2L...]: shell.execute on 'git push origin main' requires human sign-off.
   To approve, run: `dmint approve apr_9k2L...` (or use `dmint dashboard`), then retry.
   ```
2. **Human Sign-Off**: In another terminal (or via `dmint dashboard`), approve the exact request:
   ```bash
   dmint pending
   dmint approve apr_9k2L... --by alice@company.com
   ```
3. **Single-Use Retry**: Tell the agent to retry the command. `dmint hook run` verifies the Ed25519 signature against the exact RFC 8785 canonicalized arguments, atomically transitions the record from `APPROVED` to `CONSUMED`, and lets the command execute **once**.
4. **Tamper & Replay Protection**:
   - If the agent changes any argument on retry (e.g., `git push origin main --force`), the request fingerprint does not match and the call is blocked.
   - If the agent tries to run the same command a second time later, the consumed approval cannot be reused.

---

## 4. Managing Hooks (`dmint hook`)

```bash
# Check which harnesses have Dmint hooks installed in the current workspace:
dmint hook status

# Install hooks into your global home directory (~/.claude/settings.json, ~/.config/opencode/plugin/, etc.):
dmint hook install --harness claude-code --global

# Remove hooks cleanly:
dmint hook uninstall --harness all
```

---

## 5. Wrapping External MCP Servers with `dmint-mcp`

If you also connect Claude Code to external MCP servers (PostgreSQL, GitHub, Stripe), wrap them with `dmint-mcp`:

```bash
claude mcp add dmint-gateway -- dmint-mcp run --config /absolute/path/to/mcp_protection.json
```


================================================================================
DOCUMENT: OpenAI Codex CLI Integration
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/integrations/codex
SECTION: Integrations
SUMMARY: How to protect shell commands, apply_patch edits, built-in tools, and MCP calls in OpenAI Codex CLI using its dedicated codex.policy.json.
================================================================================

# OpenAI Codex CLI Integration

[OpenAI Codex CLI](https://github.com/openai/codex) dispatches local tool calls (`Bash` / `exec_command`, `apply_patch`, `read_file`, `update_plan`, `view_image`, `web_search`, and `mcp__<server>__<tool>`) through its `PreToolUse` lifecycle hook. Dmint integrates with Codex CLI via both **pre-execution hooks** (`.codex/hooks.json` and `.codex/dmint-hook.sh`) and the **`dmint-mcp` gateway**, provisioning a dedicated `.dmint/policies/codex.policy.json` tailored to Codex CLI's built-in tools.

---

## 1. One-Command Setup (`dmint init`)

In your repository root, initialize Dmint for Codex CLI:

```bash
dmint init --harness codex
```

This creates:
- `.dmint/policies/codex.policy.json` — Dedicated policy covering all built-in Codex CLI tools (`Bash`, `exec_command`, `shell`, `apply_patch`, `read_file`, `view_image`, `list_dir`, `grep_files`, `update_plan`, `web_search`, `spawn_agent`).
- `.dmint/signing.key` & `.dmint/integrity.key` (`0600`) — Local Ed25519 signing and HMAC integrity keys.
- `.codex/hooks.json` & `.codex/dmint-hook.sh` — Official `PreToolUse` hook configuration pointing directly to `.dmint/policies/codex.policy.json`.

```json title=".codex/hooks.json"
{
  "version": 1,
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash|apply_patch|mcp__.*",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "dmint hook run --harness codex --policy \"/abs/path/.dmint/policies/codex.policy.json\" --db-path \"/abs/path/.dmint/approvals.sqlite3\""
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

---

## 2. How Codex CLI Tool Calls Are Evaluated

`dmint hook run --harness codex` handles every Codex CLI tool surface:
- **Shell & Unified Exec (`Bash` / `exec_command`)**: Extracts commands whether passed as `{"command": "git status"}` or `["bash", "-lc", "git status"]` and evaluates them against both `Bash` and `shell.execute` rules in `codex.policy.json`.
- **Multi-File Unified Patches (`apply_patch`)**: Parses every `*** Add File:`, `*** Update File:`, `*** Delete File:`, and `*** Move to:` header in the patch envelope. If a single patch touches both `src/app.py` and `.env`, Dmint evaluates every path and blocks the call with `DENY`.
- **Fail-Closed `PreToolUse` Output**: Because Codex CLI `PreToolUse` enforces `"allow"` and `"deny"` (and does not enforce `"ask"`), Dmint returns `permissionDecision: "deny"` with exit code `2` whenever a call is `DENY` or `APPROVAL_REQUIRED`, ensuring unapproved commands never execute silently.

Test how your Codex policy evaluates calls from the terminal:

```bash
# Simulate a Codex Bash call:
dmint hook run --harness codex --policy .dmint/policies/codex.policy.json \
  --input '{"tool_name": "Bash", "tool_input": {"command": "git status"}}'
```

---

## 3. Approving Paused Commands

When Codex attempts an action governed by `approval_required` (such as `git push origin main`, `apply_patch` on `src/app.py`, or `docker compose up`):

1. `dmint hook run` exits with code `2`, blocking execution, and records a `PENDING` request (`apr_...`) in `.dmint/approvals.sqlite3`.
2. Review and approve the request from your terminal or web dashboard:
   ```bash
   dmint pending
   dmint approve apr_... --by dev@company.com
   ```
3. Ask Codex to retry the exact command. Dmint verifies the Ed25519 signature against the RFC 8785 fingerprint, transitions the approval to `CONSUMED`, and lets the command run once.


================================================================================
DOCUMENT: OpenCode Integration
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/integrations/opencode
SECTION: Integrations
SUMMARY: How to enforce deterministic Dmint policies and single-use human approvals in OpenCode using its dedicated opencode.policy.json and tool.execute.before plugin.
================================================================================

# OpenCode Integration

[OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) loads local TypeScript plugins from `.opencode/plugins/` (OpenCode v2) and `.opencode/plugin/` (OpenCode v1) in your workspace, or `~/.config/opencode/plugins/` globally, firing the `tool.execute.before` lifecycle hook before any tool runs.

Dmint generates a zero-dependency OpenCode guard plugin (`dmint-guard.ts`) wired to a dedicated `.dmint/policies/opencode.policy.json` that covers every built-in OpenCode tool (`bash`, `read`, `write`, `edit`, `apply_patch`, `grep`, `glob`, `list`, `lsp`, `todowrite`, `todoread`, `question`, `skill`, `task`, `webfetch`, `websearch`).

---

## 1. One-Command Setup (`dmint init`)

In your project directory, run:

```bash
# Install in current project (.opencode/plugins/dmint-guard.ts & .opencode/plugin/dmint-guard.ts):
dmint init --harness opencode

# Or install globally (~/.config/opencode/plugins/dmint-guard.ts):
dmint hook install --harness opencode --global
```

What this generates:
- `.dmint/policies/opencode.policy.json` — Dedicated policy tailored to all OpenCode built-in tools.
- `.dmint/signing.key`, `.dmint/integrity.key`, and `.dmint/approvals.sqlite3`.
- `.opencode/plugins/dmint-guard.ts` (and `.opencode/plugin/dmint-guard.ts`) — The OpenCode `tool.execute.before` guard plugin pointing to `.dmint/policies/opencode.policy.json`.

---

## 2. How the OpenCode Plugin Works

Whenever OpenCode prepares to execute a built-in or MCP tool, `dmint-guard.ts` invokes `dmint hook run --harness opencode --policy "<workspace>/.dmint/policies/opencode.policy.json"` synchronously over `stdin`:

- **`apply_patch` Inspection**: In OpenCode, `apply_patch` passes unified diffs in `output.args.patchText` with `*** Add File:`, `*** Update File:`, `*** Delete File:`, and `*** Move to:` headers. Dmint extracts and validates every file path in `patchText`.
- **Safe Built-In Session Tools**: `todowrite`, `todoread`, `question`, `grep`, `glob`, `list`, `lsp`, and `websearch` are explicitly allowed in `opencode.policy.json` so OpenCode can manage task checklists and ask clarifying questions without friction.
- **`ALLOW` (Exit `0`)**: The hook returns cleanly and OpenCode runs the tool immediately.
- **`DENY` (Exit `2`)**: The plugin throws an `Error` with the exact Dmint policy code (`DMT_POLICY_DENIED`), halting execution before the tool runs.
- **`APPROVAL_REQUIRED` (Exit `2` until approved)**: The plugin halts the tool and displays the approval ID (`apr_...`) and `dmint approve <id>` command directly in OpenCode.

---

## 3. Approving & Retrying in OpenCode

1. When OpenCode pauses on an `approval_required` action (e.g., modifying `src/index.ts` via `edit` / `apply_patch` or running `docker build` via `bash`), run in your terminal:
   ```bash
   dmint pending
   dmint approve apr_... --by dev@company.com
   ```
2. Ask OpenCode to retry the tool call. `dmint hook run` automatically verifies the Ed25519 signature for the matching RFC 8785 fingerprint, consumes the approval (`APPROVED -> CONSUMED`), and allows the tool to run once.


================================================================================
DOCUMENT: Cursor, Windsurf & Cline Integration
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/integrations/cursor
SECTION: Integrations
SUMMARY: How to protect native agent tools and MCP servers in Cursor, Windsurf, and Cline using dmint hook and dmint-mcp.
================================================================================

# Cursor, Windsurf & Cline Integration

Dmint integrates with IDE coding agents ([Cursor](https://cursor.com), Windsurf, and Cline / Roo Code) in two complementary ways:
1. **Pre-Tool Execution Hooks (`dmint hook`)**: Intercepts native IDE terminal commands (`run_terminal_cmd`, `Bash`), file reads/edits (`Read`, `Write`, `Edit`), and MCP calls via `.cursor/hooks.json`, `.windsurf/hooks.json`, and `.clinerules/hooks.json`.
2. **MCP Security Gateway (`dmint-mcp`)**: Wraps external Model Context Protocol servers (PostgreSQL, GitHub, Stripe, custom tools) in a fail-closed proxy.

---

## 1. Quick Setup for IDE Hooks (`dmint init`)

Run `dmint init` in your repository root to generate keys, a starter `policy.json` (`shell` + `filesystem` templates), and IDE hook configs:

```bash
# Configure Cursor, Windsurf, and Cline hooks in one command:
dmint init --harness cursor,windsurf,cline

# Or configure all supported harnesses at once:
dmint init --harness all
```

Test how your policy behaves before running the agent:

```bash
dmint check --tool filesystem.read_file --resource "src/app.py"      # -> ALLOW
dmint check --tool filesystem.read_file --resource ".env"            # -> DENY
dmint check --tool shell.execute --resource "git push origin main"   # -> APPROVAL_REQUIRED
```

---

## 2. Protecting External MCP Servers (`dmint-mcp`)

To wrap an MCP server (such as `@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres`) inside Cursor:

### Step A: Generate `policy.json` and `mcp_protection.json`

```bash
dmint create-mcp-policy \
  --command npx \
  --args "-y @modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres postgresql://localhost/mydb" \
  --integration-id postgres \
  -f access.md \
  -o policy.json \
  --config-output mcp_protection.json \
  -y
```

### Step B: Configure `.cursor/mcp.json`

In your project root, create or edit `.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json title=".cursor/mcp.json"
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "dmint-protected-gateway": {
      "command": "dmint-mcp",
      "args": [
        "run",
        "--config",
        "/absolute/path/to/mcp_protection.json"
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

<Tip>
Always use absolute paths in `.cursor/mcp.json` so Cursor can locate the configuration regardless of which subfolder is open.
</Tip>

---

## 3. Approving Paused Tool Calls

When an IDE agent triggers an `APPROVAL_REQUIRED` rule (via either `dmint hook` or `dmint-mcp`):

1. Execution pauses before the tool runs, and a `PENDING` record (`apr_...`) is written to `.dmint/approvals.sqlite3` (or your configured `approval_db`).
2. Approve from your terminal or local web dashboard:
   ```bash
   # Option A: Terminal CLI
   dmint pending
   dmint approve apr_abc123... --by dev@company.com

   # Option B: Local Web Dashboard
   dmint dashboard
   ```
3. Ask the agent in Cursor/Windsurf/Cline to retry the exact tool call. Dmint automatically looks up the approved assertion matching the request's RFC 8785 fingerprint, consumes it atomically (`APPROVED -> CONSUMED`), and executes the call once.


================================================================================
DOCUMENT: Windsurf & Cline / Roo Code
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/integrations/windsurf-cline
SECTION: Integrations
SUMMARY: How to protect native IDE tools and MCP servers in Windsurf Cascade, Cline, and Roo Code using their dedicated per-harness policy files.
================================================================================

# Windsurf Cascade & Cline / Roo Code Integration

Dmint provides first-class pre-execution hooks and dedicated built-in tool policies for **Windsurf Cascade** (`.windsurf/hooks.json`) and **Cline / Roo Code** (`.clinerules/hooks/PreToolUse`, `.cline/hooks/PreToolUse.sh`, and `.clinerules/hooks.json`).

---

## 1. Install Pre-Tool Hooks (`dmint init`)

From your workspace root, run:

```bash
# Install hooks and dedicated policies for both Windsurf and Cline / Roo Code:
dmint init --harness windsurf,cline
```

This creates:
- **Windsurf Cascade**:
  - `.dmint/policies/windsurf.policy.json` — Dedicated policy for Windsurf Cascade's pre-hooks (`pre_run_command`, `pre_read_code`, `pre_write_code`, `pre_mcp_tool_use`, `pre_user_prompt`) and native tools.
  - `.windsurf/hooks.json` — Official Windsurf Cascade hook configuration registering `pre_run_command`, `pre_read_code`, `pre_write_code`, and `pre_mcp_tool_use` with `show_output: true` and blocking disallowed actions via exit code `2`.
- **Cline (VS Code Extension & CLI) / Roo Code**:
  - `.dmint/policies/cline.policy.json` — Dedicated policy covering all Cline built-in tools (`run_commands`, `execute_command`, `read_files`, `read_file`, `editor`, `write_to_file`, `replace_in_file`, `apply_patch`, `search_files`, `list_files`, `list_code_definition_names`, `ask_followup_question`, `attempt_completion`, `new_task`, `switch_mode`, `browser_action`, `use_mcp_tool`).
  - `.clinerules/hooks/PreToolUse` — Executable hook script (no extension, `chmod +x`) required by the Cline VS Code extension.
  - `.cline/hooks/PreToolUse.sh` — Executable hook script required by the Cline CLI.
  - `.clinerules/hooks.json` — Declarative hook configuration for Roo Code compatibility.
- `.dmint/` — Local Ed25519 signing key (`0600`), HMAC integrity key (`0600`), and `approvals.sqlite3` database.

Verify installed hooks and their dedicated policy paths at any time:

```bash
dmint hook status
```

---

## 2. Official Payload & Output Schemas Handled by Dmint

### Windsurf Cascade (`.windsurf/hooks.json`)
Windsurf Cascade sends `agent_action_name` (`pre_run_command`, `pre_read_code`, `pre_write_code`, `pre_mcp_tool_use`) and `tool_info` (`command_line`, `file_path`, `mcp_server_name`, `mcp_tool_name`, `mcp_tool_arguments`) over `stdin`. Dmint normalizes `tool_info` automatically and exits with code `2` (writing the reason to `stderr`) whenever a call is `DENY` or `APPROVAL_REQUIRED`.

### Cline VS Code Extension & CLI (`.clinerules/hooks/PreToolUse` & `.cline/hooks/PreToolUse.sh`)
Cline sends either the VS Code extension payload (`{"preToolUse": {"toolName": "...", "parameters": {...}}}` with JSON-stringified parameter values) or the CLI payload (`{"tool_call": {"name": "...", "input": {...}}}`).
- Dmint automatically parses stringified JSON parameters, inspects every file in batch `read_files` / `apply_patch` calls and every command in batch `run_commands` (`{"commands": [...]}`) calls, and returns `{"cancel": false}` on `ALLOW` or `{"cancel": true, "errorMessage": "..."}` when blocked.
- Turn-completion and question tools (`attempt_completion`, `ask_followup_question`) are explicitly allowed in `cline.policy.json` so Cline can ask questions and finish tasks cleanly.

---

## 3. Approving Paused Requests

When Windsurf or Cline pauses on an `APPROVAL_REQUIRED` action:

```bash
# Review pending requests in terminal:
dmint pending

# Approve once:
dmint approve apr_... --by dev@company.com

# Or review in the web dashboard:
dmint dashboard
```

When the agent retries the exact same tool call, Dmint verifies the Ed25519 assertion, marks it `CONSUMED`, and allows the action to proceed once.

DOCUMENT: Google Antigravity & Gemini CLI
URL: https://docs.dmint.app/integrations/antigravity

SUMMARY: How to enforce deterministic security in Google Antigravity (AGY) and Gemini CLI workflows.
